The app targets merchants that primarily need PO creation, inventory planning, receiving, transfers, stocktakes, landed cost calculations, supplier/product data, and low-stock email alerts, without requiring a full WMS or ERP. Key fit criteria are emphasized: it is embedded in Shopify, depends on Shopify location inventory and order history, and is best for finished-goods sellers whose sales and inventory mostly flow through Shopify. It is not positioned for businesses needing raw material tracking, bundle component tracking, or heavy external marketplace workflows unless that data syncs into Shopify. The app supports reorder suggestions using inventory levels, inbound stock, sales velocity, growth assumptions, lead times, and target coverage days, plus manual/ad hoc PO creation. Receiving can be handled through manual entry, barcode scanning, or CSV upload. A follow-up response highlights a separate paid managed migration and audit service for merchants needing help with multi-location synchronization, inventory adjustments, and cleanup of historical discrepancies. No final decision or resolution is reached; the thread remains promotional and informational. sthich August 5, 2026, 6:30am 1 Stocky’s sunset is just over 3 weeks out and, given the bump in installs of our app this past week, I venture to guess that there are still many merchants holding out or still searching for the right alternative. I want to take this opportunity to showcase (offer) our app that may legitimately be the best solution for a meaningful cohort of merchants migrating from Stocky. It’s called Alfred Purchase Orders . I’m a DTC Shopify e-commerce founder ( Capy ) with a prior background in building software for both startups and big tech, and this past year we built Alfred Purchase Orders. Originally, it was an app designed to meet our own use cases for demand forecasting, PO creation, and receiving inventory efficiently. However, we made the decision to scale it up into a public app this Spring after the Stocky sunset announcement. From personal experience, I knew there was a major gap in available solutions on the market that sits between simple PO/forecasting apps and the expensive and heavy enterprise solutions. That’s ultimately why I decided to make it available to other merchants as an app on the Shopify app store. Alfred Purchase Orders may be good fit for your store if you: Need primarily purchase orders & inventory management : Alfred is a lightweight but powerful platform to analyze inventory/sales data, forecast stockouts, create reusable PO templates, generate & manage POs, and manage inventory (receive POs, transfer stock, stocktakes, and adjustments). Alfred is not a WMS or ERP and does not aspire to be one. Are Shopify-first : Alfred is an Shopify admin embedded app (no standalone web app or portal), and operates/depends on Shopify Location inventory and Order data for historical sales velocity (and forecasting). If current inventory data or a large segment of your sales/orders do not live in or flow through Shopify, Alfred won’t be a good match for you. For example, if you’re heavy on Amazon/Walmart and your inventory/sales data does not sync into/flow into Shopify, Alfred won’t be a complete solution for you. This app was designed for stores that live and operate on Shopify. Sell finished goods : You order from suppliers/distributors and sell finished goods and products. Alfred does not track raw materials and supplies, and currently does not offer support for bundles made up of other product variants. Have fewer than 30k product variants in your catalog : While our documentation communicates a 20k variant cap on top plan, our infrastructure has scaled to support ~30k product variant catalogs. Alfred does excluded archived products and offer a “Catalog exclusion” feature that enables you to define rules for Alfred to exclude products from syncing and using variant quota. If your store has over 30K product variants, Alfred won’t be able to perform consistently and we don’t recommend selecting it as your Stocky replacement. You can blame Shopify API rate-limiting for that . Key features to highlight Product Planner : Alfred offers a module for inventory and sales reporting, as well as product performance reporting, which includes frameworks like ABC-XYZ, Fast-Slow-NonMoving, and more. This report helps you quickly identify and annotate products you should keep stocked or products that are dragging down performance and taking up capital and warehouse space. Purchase Order Planner (PO templates) : Alfred offers 3 primary PO plans or reusable templates - Standard PO, Min/Max Replenishment, and Meet Forecasted Demand. Standard PO leaves the reorder quantities to you but surfaces useful inventory and sales data in a single view (current inventory, inbound inventory, unit sales last 7/14/30, MOQ, Pack Size, etc.). Min/Max Replenishment is the classic min/max(target) unit calculations based on product+location-specific min and max thresholds you define. Meet Forecasted Demand is Alfred’s approach to “smart” or automated reorder quantity calculations and suggestions based on: current inventory, inbound inventory, historical sales velocity, a user-provided growth (+/-)%, order lead times, and your desired target inventory coverage days. Additionally, a “ad hoc PO” option exists where the user is given an empty PO and filters+selects products from the catalog and enters unit quantities, which is perfect for small/straightforward orders where you know exactly what and how many unit you’d like to order. Receiving POs, Transfers, Stocktakes : Alfred makes it incredibly simple to receive POs (or shipments within a PO) in just a few clicks. From the PO page you can launch into a “receiving session” and indicate which items to officially receive into Shopify inventory by manual unit entry, barcode scanning (single item or carton), or a CSV upload. There’s also a quick “populate all expected units” button to speed through receiving on batches where you’ve already counted and everything is as expected. Transfers & Stocktakes follow a similar interface and also support manual, barcode, and CSV upload entry. Landed Costs & Profit Margins : Alfred enables you to enter order level additional costs & credits (shipping/freight, customs, discounts) with multiple allocation (to line items) models, and calculates landed costs for each line item on a PO. You can quickly publish landed costs directly to Shopify (unit costs) and/or update a product’s sell/list price in Shopify directly from the PO. There’s also a “Pricing & Margin” module that enables you to publish updated landed costs and list prices across many or all items in a PO in a single action. Supplier & Supplied Products data : Alfred has a Suppliers module that enables you to define supplier<>product associations and also define attributes like MOQ, lead time, pack size/quantity, which fast+facilitates accurate PO plan quantity calculations/recommendations. Inventory Summary & Low Stock email alerts : Alfred supports custom configured email alerts for inventory digests/summaries as well as low stock/reorder point emails (based on units or weeks of supply). Configure alerts for specific vendors, tags, collections, or specific products to ensure you’re keeping your high-performing products in stock. Pricing Alfred offers a 30-day trial with plans that range from $29 to $99 per month (or 10% off with annual plan) depending on product variant count and estimated annualized revenue. Yes, there are a few “alternatives” on the market that are either actually low-priced ( Alfred Migration page (you can request a demo here if you’d like!) Stock > Alfred data migration reference Thanks and good luck with migration! For a lot of merchants migrating right now under the August deadline, the biggest bottleneck isn’t just generating the PO—it’s ensuring multi-location state synchronization, handling complex adjustments, and cleaning up historical ledger drift without spending hours manually auditing spreadsheets. title: Removing Stocky is a Material Retail Operations Risk
text: Removing Stocky is a Material Retail Operations Risk = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Removing Stocky is a Material Retail Operations Risk Retail & Point of Sale troubleshooting AI-generated summary Shopify’s planned removal of Stocky is being framed as a serious operational risk for retail merchants using Shopify POS Pro. The main concern is that Stocky supports core workflows such as purchase orders, receiving, stocktakes, supplier data, inventory adjustments, and reporting, while Shopify’s native replacement is described as incomplete or not yet available for key functions like stock counts. Several merchants say the change creates major burdens, including manually recreating supplier and historical data, losing cost-history visibility, and paying for third-party tools to replace features that were previously included. Some report that this decision, combined with other POS changes, has pushed them to trial or move to other POS systems such as Lightspeed. Recent replies focus on practical migration risks and alternatives. Multiple app developers or vendors suggested replacement tools for purchase orders, transfers, inventory visibility, or cost history. A key warning is that Stocky data access has a deadline: after August 31, Stocky becomes read-only for about 90 days, supplier records cannot be exported, and purchase orders must be exported one CSV at a time. The issue remains unresolved, with merchants still asking Shopify for feature parity, migration tooling, and clearer continuity plans. petgrocer February 20, 2026, 8:09pm 1 Open Letter to Shopify Leadership and Board of Directors Subject: Shopify’s decision to remove Stocky is a material retail operations risk — and it requires immediate intervention To Shopify Leadership and the Board of Directors, Shopify has confirmed that Stocky will no longer be available after August 31, 2026 , and that it was delisted from the Shopify App Store on February 2, 2026 , meaning merchants cannot reinstall it. For many retail merchants, this is not a simple product cleanup. It is the removal of core operating infrastructure. Why this decision is operationally dangerous Shopify’s own documentation describes Stocky as an inventory management tool included with Shopify POS Pro , used for: forecasting inventory needs, suggesting what to order, inventory counts, and inventory transfers. Shopify also documents that Stocky supports critical day-to-day workflows such as: purchase orders (create, manage, track, and receive), stocktakes (manual or barcode-based), with adjustments syncing back to Shopify, and Stocky reporting , including low-stock and ordering-related reporting. These are not edge features. They are the mechanics of running a physical retail business. When these workflows are weakened or removed before a proven replacement is ready, the result is immediate: receiving delays count errors purchasing mistakes margin erosion staff inefficiency and avoidable operational disruption Shopify’s migration guidance confirms major gaps Shopify’s migration page explicitly acknowledges several risks and limitations: Stocky data does not automatically migrate into Shopify (including old purchase orders and stocktakes). Merchants must manually export records they want to keep. Suppliers cannot be exported from Stocky. Some Stocky features “might work differently” or “might not yet be available” in Shopify. Stocky APIs stop working on August 31, 2026 , requiring third-party integration changes. Most concerning: Shopify’s own feature comparison says “Perform inventory stock counts” is “Not available yet – improvements in progress” on the Shopify side. That is a direct admission that feature parity is not complete. Merchant feedback already shows real business impact Shopify Community threads are already documenting what merchants are losing or struggling to replace, including: purchase order creation and receiving, average-cost workflows, barcode-based stock counts, and label printing or basic count workflows without taking on major new software costs. In one thread, a merchant reports support guidance effectively pushing them toward ERP-level replacements costing roughly $350–$1,000+ per month , after previously relying on Stocky for “90% of the lift.” This is not a smooth migration. It is a cost transfer and workflow downgrade. Why shareholders and the board should care Shopify’s own 2025 results make this a governance issue, not just a product issue. In Shopify’s Feb. 11, 2026 earnings release, the company highlighted: 30% full-year revenue growth 29% GMV growth 27% offline revenue growth $1.5B operating income $2.0B free cash flow If Shopify is publicly emphasizing offline and omnichannel momentum, then removing a mission-critical retail operations tool before full replacement is ready creates risk in a segment it is actively relying on for growth. This creates four clear shareholder risks: Retail merchant churn risk POS-heavy merchants are harder to win and expensive to lose. Operational breakage is one of the fastest ways to drive churn. Merchant concerns are already visible in Shopify’s own community. POS Pro revenue and retention risk Stocky functionality is tied to POS Pro retail workflows in Shopify’s documentation (including stocktakes and reports). Weakening those workflows undermines confidence in Shopify’s retail stack. Platform trust erosion Shopify is asking merchants to migrate while simultaneously stating that key records won’t migrate automatically, suppliers can’t be exported, APIs will break, and some features are not yet available. That damages platform trust. Higher support and ecosystem costs Merchants are already being pushed toward workarounds, paid third-party tools, and fragmented workflows. That increases support burden and partner friction rather than simplifying operations. What the board should require immediately This is fixable, but only if Shopify pauses and corrects course. 1) Pause the Stocky sunset until feature parity is real Do not remove Stocky until Shopify can fully support the core retail workflows merchants use every day. 2) Publish a dated feature-parity roadmap Include delivery dates for: purchase orders receiving workflows barcode-based stock counting / stocktakes supplier/vendor continuity reporting parity retail label and receiving workflows 3) Guarantee data continuity Provide a practical migration path for: historical purchase orders stocktakes supplier records reporting continuity Manual CSV exports are not a true operational replacement. 4) Create a POS-heavy retail advisory group Test replacement workflows with real multi-location retailers before deprecating Stocky. I specifically want to be a part of this test so our feedback is directly heard. 5) Report migration impact internally and to investors Track and disclose (where appropriate): POS Pro retention migration success rates support volume related to inventory workflow transitions churn in affected cohorts Final point Shopify has built its reputation on helping merchants operate and scale with confidence. Removing Stocky before a complete, proven replacement exists sends the opposite signal: that retail operational continuity is secondary to internal product simplification. For merchants, that is unacceptable. For shareholders, it is unnecessary risk. This decision should be reconsidered immediately. Suggested alternatives included: Cin7 Core, Katana, QuickBooks Commerce, and SKULabs, all described as supporting reason-based stock adjustments and historical reporting. Prediko was mentioned specifically for its transfer feature, which one participant said Stocky lacked. SKUSavvy received the most detailed follow-up, presented as a Stocky-like warehouse management option with detailed action logs, custom adjustment reasons, historical reporting, batch/lot tracking, barcode workflows, returns handling, and Shopify integration. Current state: No clear final decision was made; the discussion remains open. The only direct response from the original poster was thanks for the suggestions. Screenshots were shared to illustrate SKUSavvy’s logging and interface, but no independent comparison or confirmed outcome was provided. Tarrah28 March 16, 2025, 10:26am 1 I am after an alternative to Stocky as it is constantly causing us headaches. In an alternative however we must be able to adjust stock with a reason (I.e. Expired, Returned to Supplier, Donations) and download reports of adjustments for the past 12 months. Any assistance narrowing down alternatives would be greatly appreciated. SKULabs, Cin7 Core, Katana, and QuickBooks Commerce all offer stock adjustments with reason tracking (e.g., expired, returned, donated) and detailed reports for 12+ months. Logs include: Complete warehouse log Order logs (purchase orders, outbound orders, transfers) Employee logs bin logs SKU logs Stock take logs Batch logs kingstore_0-1750013862314.png 1527×820 71.5 KB kingstore_0-1750012721978.png 1541×830 155 KB Stock adjustments are easily done by scan, search, or simply tapping the quantity and can require a custom reason. My business doesn’t distinguish between vendors and suppliers when purchasing so going to Shopify’s native purchase order interface also means creating supplier profiles for all the vendors even though all of my products are already associated with the correct vendors. Has anyone made an app that does EXACTLY what stocky does? I’m desperate for a budget option that can generate POs from specific vendors and utilize filters during generation. Thanks! DougInOr June 10, 2026, 10:27pm 2 Exactly, no. That would flirt with trademark/copyright infringement. However, FyreTrail is likely something you need to look into simply because it handles the Purchase Order flow really well. The key difference between Stocky and FyreTrail is that Stocky (as I see it) handled Shopify’s product catalog for retailers whereas FyreTrail handles retailers and removes the concern about Shopify’s catalog from retailers. FyreTrail approaches the process for retailers who need to order products from their Suppliers. It recognizes a “Vendor” really is a Supplier (who sells the item to you) and a Brand (what sells to a Supplier or you) and doesn’t do the silly things that Stocky does with making you choose a Supplier or a Vendor when creating a PO. On top of that, it also recognizes that your Products shouldn’t have to be recreated 15 times to get them into Shopify. Do it once - on the PO and doesn’t force you to enter the things you don’t need to know to get a product ordered. Worry about that when it gets here and when you’re ready to sell it, not when you want to order it. So, FyreTrail is process oriented… to YOUR process… with a little help along the way. Give it a look then reach out if you have any questions. oscprofessional June 11, 2026, 12:34pm 3 Hi @MurphysBootShop , Apps Similar to Stocky Lokad (formerly known for demand forecasting) PO generation from vendors Inventory-based filters Budget: ~$200-500/month (not cheap) Infoplus (Inventory + PO Management) Vendor-based PO generation Advanced filtering Budget: ~$300+/month TraceLink for Shopify (Enterprise) Supply chain PO management Vendor management Budget: Custom pricing (pricey) SealSubs-Roan June 14, 2026, 5:12am 5 MurphysBootShop: The sundowning of Stocky in August feels like a nightmare right now. My business doesn’t distinguish between vendors and suppliers when purchasing so going to Shopify’s native purchase order interface also means creating supplier profiles for all the vendors even though all of my products are already associated with the correct vendors. Has anyone made an app that does EXACTLY what stocky does? I’m desperate for a budget option that can generate POs from specific vendors and utilize filters during generation. Hey there @MurphysBootShop Several merchants share that the best way around this is to abandon Stocky’s vendor system and use vendor tags or metafields to organize the product information, and then place the orders through a third party system that uses filtering logic. Solutions like Cin7 Core, Sumtracker, or Katana are usually the best alternatives to Stocky’s PO creation and vendor-specific filtering. They provide you the ability to group products dynamically and generate POs without having to recreate supplier records as you must on the Shopify native app. And if you really want to keep it light, using tagged products with bulk export apps like Matrixify (formerly Excelify) can also simulate the basics of a PO workflow. Pipokx June 14, 2026, 8:55am 6 Hey @MurphysBootShop , What type of business do you run and what volumes you process ? Depending on your business specificities, some apps will be better than others, or sometimes, no apps at all are needed as jobs can be done in the background using logic and syncs between your systems. Tell us a bit more about your business and workflow, Thanks MurphysBootShop June 18, 2026, 5:32pm 7 I run a small shoe store which means that frequently I am ordering 2-12 pairs at a time. Currently when using Stocky: I will select a vendor, under “forecast type” I use “target stock level” and set it to 1, apply a filter to only add items with a relevant tag, and then create the PO. Being able to limit my PO’s reach by tags is crucial as my store’s inventory contains dozens of styles and odd sizes I normally have no intention of ordering. kingstore June 19, 2026, 8:43pm 8 I’m certainly biased but the best solution for the Stocky sunset is SKUSavvy. Stocky has a lot of logic based components and SKUSavvy is designed to mimic nearly exactly what stocky does. This includes automated purchase orders with min/max levels, automated allocation of stock across your locations, check-in barcode scanning and printing, complete inventory management with 3D bin mapping and bin-to-bin replenishment, as well as guided pick routing, fulfillment and shipping automation. Additionally, SKUSavvy is perfectly integrated with Shopify providing a dual way sync across all key data types and for all Shopify versions and POS. While this is not a perfect replacement, if you are looking for the de facto replacement for Stocky, this will certainly do it. This is not free, so its hard to complete there, but at $179/month for a full WMS, this is also not break the bank type of system. Give it a try for free or explore the website MurphysBootShop July 8, 2026, 3:00pm 9 Yeah, I’m not even gonna remotely consider a solution that costs more than $100 per month. We pay so much for shopify already, I can’t justify more than $1000 to our yearly operating costs for a piece of functionality that used to be free on this POS and our previous system. kthoppae July 9, 2026, 3:38pm 12 that makes sense. It sounds like the biggest hurdle isn’t learning a new purchasing workflow it’s having to recreate operational relationships that already existed. If your replenishment process already knows which products belong to which vendor, having to manually assign suppliers across the catalog before you can even generate a PO creates a lot of upfront work before you see any benefit. It seems like preserving those supplier relationships during the transition is almost as important as the PO functionality itself. MurphysBootShop July 9, 2026, 3:53pm 13 I agree. But I transitioned to Shopify 3 years ago and I can’t really start over. What do you recommend? kthoppae July 9, 2026, 4:19pm 14 That’s a tough spot, and I probably wouldn’t start over by manually rebuilding everything either. If I were evaluating replacements today, I’d focus less on feature checklists and more on migration effort. A few questions I’d ask are: • Can it preserve or import existing supplier relationships? • Can it generate POs using the workflow I’m already familiar with? • Does it support receiving and inventory updates without adding extra manual work? • How much catalog setup is required before I can create my first PO? If a solution requires weeks of rebuilding master data before it delivers value, that migration cost becomes part of the decision too. Out of curiosity, roughly how many SKUs are you managing today? DougInOr July 9, 2026, 9:23pm 15 I’m going to tack on to @kthoppae 's evaluation, but I really think any valid solution needs to give you an easy way to transition from Stocky. The caveat to you not wanting to spend money on an app for features that used to be free with Pro is that many inexpensive solutions don’t offer an easy transition system. And, if they do, the functionality you need is lacking. I’m not calling any single app out at all (I’m not even thinking of any), but the reality just boils down to how much money an app needs to make simply to be viable. Ok, so it’s a tradeoff… you want an easy transition? Might be hard to find an app that gives you this and gives you the features you NEED for the cost that you’re willing to digest. I’m not trying to get you to come to FyreTrail… I’m really not. I would love to have you, but if FyreTrail is not something you’re even wanting to look at because it costs money then I get it - your priority is then budget and that’s completely fair and understandable. But… what it does do is save you time both in the migration (we have one) and the day to day uses that it will very likely pay for itself many times over. Ultimately it’s totally your choice to either take that risk after the 14 day free trial or recognize it during the trial and take advantage of it afterwards. So what if it’s not FyreTrail? Evaluate, weigh your options, weigh the amount of work you do now and in the future, then decide, “Is this worth my money given what it does for me?” Then choose the app or direction that meets those needs best. You’re first, your store is first, not some app (yes, even my app) that can’t meet those needs. text: Stocky Sunset = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Stocky Sunset - Why doesn't Shopify Native PO have the same functionality? Shopify Apps shopify-developed-apps AI-generated summary A Canadian art supply store preparing for Stocky’s August 31 sunset says Shopify’s native purchase orders are not a sufficient replacement, especially for large POs with hundreds of product variants. Key missing functions listed include default tax rates, pack sizes, per-supplier currency conversion, customizable PO columns, demand-based PO generation, supplier/vendor linking, PO merging, forecasting, and easier quantity entry. Several replies focus on possible replacement approaches. Some app developers disclose their affiliation and describe tools that address parts of the gap, including supplier-level tax defaults, pack sizes, currency handling, forecasting, landed cost, and large-PO workflows; others note that building and distributing a replacement app before the deadline may be difficult. A recurring technical point is that Shopify’s native PO system appears rooted in inventory transfers rather than supplier-based purchasing, which may explain why supplier defaults are absent. Later comments ask which pain point is worst—tax, currency, or pack sizes—and suggest testing any tool with a representative 300-line PO. No resolution is reached; the main question remains what dependable Stocky replacement can handle complex supplier purchasing at reasonable cost. WyndhamArt June 18, 2026, 9:38pm 1 We’re a Canadian art supply store preparing to migrate from Stocky before it is sunset on August 31, and have been trying to find a replacement for the app but only been met with disappointment or frustration. Most of the 3rd party apps were missing crucial features, or were asking us to pay $30-$50 a month for something as simple as currency conversion. We have turned back to the native Shopify POs as at least that’s free, but have also been very disappointed with it. We would like Shopify to reconsider sunsetting Stocky, or at least extend the Stocky sunset deadline until their native PO is as functional. Here are some features missing from Shopify Native POs off the top of my head: Default tax rate Stocky allowed a global default tax rate applied to all new POs automatically. Shopify requires entering a tax rate per line item, which is very frustrating when creating POs with hundreds of variants (which is most of our orders as we have single lines of paint with many hundreds of colour options) Pack sizes Stocky had a pack size field, so we’d know how many of each item we needed to order. There is no equivalent in Shopify POs, which would require us to either memorize that information for every item (not possible with our number of SKUs) or keep some separate spreadsheet with all that product information. Currency cost conversion Stocky shows converted costs when a supplier invoiced us in a different currency. In Shopify, it will only show the converted total, meaning I’d have to either convert before entering the price, or do it line by line after, in order to enter the accurate cost and calculate pricing. Customizable PO columns Stocky allowed you to display sales data and current stock levels directly on the PO, along side other helpful information. Shopify POs have no such customization. Demand-based PO generation Stocky could generate POs based on sales, or minimum stock numbers. Shopify’s native POs do not allow you to generate POs at all, and the actual workflow to add items into a PO, especially a large number of them, is very clunky. Supplier and Vendor linking Stocky allowed us to link vendors under a supplier, and then would only show products associated with those vendors when we were putting together POs. With Shopify, we have to filter based on vendor, which requires us to either remember every vendor and their associated supplier, or keep a spreadsheet of supplier information. No Merging POs Stocky allowed us to merge POs. Shopify does not. No product forecasting Stocky gives us an A B or C rating for our products, based on their recent sales. Shopify POs have nothing like this. Adding items and THEN changing quantities When adding items into Stocky POs, we could decide the quantity at the same time. With Shopify, we need to add the item and then change the quantity. I’ll cut myself here before this gets too long! We don’t understand why Stocky is being sunset when no other app meets it’s quality or ease of use. We had our frustrations with Stocky as well, but now looking at what the alternatives are, we appreciate how far ahead of anything else it really is! Note: Please do not advertise your app to me on this post! (If you are a real user of an app you like, with no affiliation, feel free mention it! I think we’ve looked at all the major ones at this point, but maybe there’s something we missed or overlooked.) Bloom_Analytics June 24, 2026, 6:33am 2 Can you please share the apps you have tried so far? Would be helpful for me to look for other options MyWorks July 9, 2026, 10:57pm 6 @WyndhamArt just wanted to add a comment here that’s hopefully helpful - as this isn’t a paid app suggestion. With Stocky going away, and our own users asking us for a robust way to handle POs and light inventory management / reordering with Shopify; we decided to build our own solution, but for free. We’ve build in features that already include exactly what you’ve shared above: full tax rate support, currency conversion, stock levels, demand-based PO generation, super clean supplier management, forecasting, and quite easy PO creation. Check it out at Stockroom - Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Unlimited purchase orders, receiving & sync with QuickBooks | Shopify App Store - we’re making it completely free for everyone! We think Shopify merchants deserve a robust, stable and long term way to handle Purchase Orders (and the re-ordering/receiving processes that come with them) in a way that fits their business, and not at an additional cost. We’d love to hear any feedback from you as we continue to build more features to make this a helpful home for Shopify store merchants coming from Stocky! irish.chen July 13, 2026, 7:22am 7 Reading through this thread + a couple others on the Stocky sunset — trying to figure out if it’s worth building a lean replacement instead of another bloated all-in-one. If you’ve got 60 seconds: which of these would you actually pay for — Bulk PO creation (100+ line items at once) Receiving multiple POs from one shipment without opening each one individually Tax rate / pack size / currency conversion handled automatically instead of typed per line Reorder suggestions based on lead time, not just “you’re low on stock” A wizard that pulls your old Stocky data + suppliers over before Aug 31 Also curious — what pushed you away from the apps you already tried? No pitch here, just trying not to build the wrong thing. Happy to add you to an early access list if any of this is useful once it exists. AlfredCommerce July 14, 2026, 9:11pm 8 It’s honestly a slog. Trust me. I built an alternative for my own DTC store (Capy) and decided to scale up due to the sunset announcement + launched publicly back in May. Building great workflows and solutions for niches that Stocky once handled hasn’t been the issue. Distribution and getting more merchants to pay you any attention has been. I have a handful of stores on it hammering away for hoursss a week and love it, but getting visibility with merchants is the challenge. So if you’re trying to build and sell/market with the sunset looking less than 2 months out I’d seriously consider how large your window will be. Just my 2 cents. HJBCodeforge July 31, 2026, 8:23pm 9 Disclosure: I build one of the replacement apps, so I have an interest here. I’m replying because your three specific gaps are unusually concrete and I can answer them directly rather than vaguely. On the underlying “why”: native POs grew out of the transfers feature, which models moving stock between locations. Purchasing concerns — a supplier’s default tax treatment, their pack sizes, their currency — belong to the supplier , and transfers has no supplier entity to hang them on. That’s why they’re per-line or absent rather than defaulted, and it’s also why “add a default tax rate” isn’t a small patch for them. Against your list, for what mine does: Default tax rate — held on the supplier. Lines left blank inherit it, so a several-hundred-line PO doesn’t mean typing a rate several hundred times. Pack size — a per-line field, so ordering in cases rather than units is explicit on the order. Currency — per supplier, not per store. Your USD paint supplier and a CAD supplier sit side by side without you converting anything by hand. I’d rather be straight about the cost point you raised, since it’s the part that clearly annoyed you: mine is $29/month for the paid tier, which is inside the $30–50 band you’re objecting to, not below it. There’s a free tier that includes the whole PO and receiving workflow plus CSV import and export, capped at 5 open purchase orders at a time — which, given you’re doing large variant-heavy orders rather than many concurrent ones, may actually cover you. Worth testing before assuming you need to pay. Whatever you land on, the useful test for a catalogue like yours is a single PO with a few hundred variant lines. Most tools are fine at 10 lines and become unusable at 300 — pagination, page reloads on every edit, totals recalculating on the server. That’s a five-minute test and it eliminates most of the field faster than any feature comparison. App Store: Replenora - Purchase orders, receiving, and reorder points in one place | Shopify App Store More detail: https://replenora.hjbcodeforge.com Tomer_Kaya September 3, 2026, 7:47pm 10 @WyndhamArt I’m not with Shopify and I’m not selling anything, just trying to understand how retailers are coping since 31 August. You mentioned entering a tax rate per line item on POs with hundreds of paint variants. On a typical order of that size, is the per-line tax entry what costs you the most — or is it the currency conversion? Thanks. Denyslg September 5, 2026, 4:28am 11 The currency answer has a second layer, and it bites later than the typing does. Which rate, and on which day. A USD invoice converted at the rate the day you raised the order is a different cost from the same invoice converted the day the paint landed, and different again from what your bank gave you when the payment cleared, and across a six-week lead time three to five percent between those three dates is an ordinary month. Pick one and write the rule down. The cost you store drives every margin calculation for a year. Rate at receipt is the defensible choice for retail, since that is when the asset arrived, and it matches landed cost, which nobody here has raised: freight, duty and brokerage spread over the lines by value rather than by carton, because duty follows value. Disclosure: I build Binly ( Binly ‑ Stocktake & Reorder - Stocky replacement: phone stocktakes, POs & smart reorder | Shopify App Store ), which does landed cost and per-delivery costs. It has no default tax rate per supplier, so your first complaint stands unanswered. vizuliiss September 23, 2026, 6:59pm 12 No app pitch, just curious with hundreds of variants, how are you currently catching it when a per-line tax rate or pack size is wrong? Manual spot-checks, or does something flag it for you? Jack_BuildsShopify September 24, 2026, 12:44am 13 For hundreds of colour variants per PO, I would separate reusable supplier data from PO-line calculations. Keep currency, default tax, pack size/MOQ and supplier SKU mapping in one master record, then let each PO inherit those values and only surface exceptions. I would also test one representative large PO by exporting the current SKU, pack-size and cost data first, then compare the native PO result line by line so you know exactly which fields are lost. Of pack size, tax rate and currency conversion, which one creates the most manual work on a typical PO today? text: Why Stocky should remain = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Why Stocky should remain - An executive position Shopify Plus stocky , inventory-management AI-generated summary Shopify Plus merchants are strongly objecting to Shopify sunsetting Stocky, arguing that native Shopify Purchase Orders are not a functional replacement for real inventory operations. Key concerns include loss of scanner-based stock counts, variance review, supplier-aware workflows, order-to-PO conversion, PO consolidation by vendor, direct PO emailing, cost memory, landed/actual cost tracking, demand forecasting, stock valuation reports, and integrations with accounting tools such as QuickBooks or MYOB. Your Concern Status Notes Min/Max replenishment Not planned for 2026 Recommend Inventory apps Generate PO based on inventory settings Not planned for 2026 Recommend Inventory apps Pre-populate supplier level PO at supplier level Available now All recommended apps include supplier management Custom fields/status designations Not available Tags can serve as partial workaround Supplier code on POs Not currently available Gap for now - but our team are working on this area Bulk CSV import for purchase orders Not currently available All recommended PO apps support CSV import: muttsonline February 18, 2026, 11:30pm 10 I believe most of us are not interested in paying for yet - another app - to be able to complete tasks that should be native to the system we already pay for. muttsonline February 18, 2026, 11:31pm 11 It is beyond comprehension. To me these changes are sending a very clear message to us - and that is - we don’t care what you need to operate…we just got you all locked into contracts and increasing costs….and functionality loss…just pay for yet another app. muttsonline February 18, 2026, 11:32pm 12 AGREE! Huge middle finger to us. DougInOr February 18, 2026, 11:36pm 13 Thank you. Makes total sense - I’m not pushing to use apps, I’m pushing to save time and money based on my own personal experience. My standpoint is; if you’re already paying for a service that does not provide the services you need, why would you not simply ditch that service and replace it with another one that not only better meets your needs, but is also likely overall cheaper because of the time it saves you? To me, if an app - whatever app - saves you say 6 hours per week at roughly $20/hr in labor (I’m just using an easy number - not sure if that’s high or low) then that’s $120/wk or $480/month in savings for spending $59/month or even $159/month?? Even taking the highest tier still saves money, but if you’re at that level, you’re already saving way more than 6hrs/wk. So to me, it’s very strange someone says that’s not a good deal. At any rate, thanks for that update… I’m wondering what their “recommended inventory apps” are. Philip_Gangi May 2, 2026, 9:09pm 16 There was nothing fundamentally wrong with Stocky. The Native PO system is fundamentally incomplete. It is not ready to be used mainstream. kthoppae May 4, 2026, 2:57am 17 That’s a good way to put it it’s not that something broke, it’s that the replacement never fully covered what people were actually using day to day. Stocky worked because the PO lifecycle stayed connected from purchasing to receiving to inventory and reporting. Once that connection is missing, even basic workflows start to feel incomplete, especially at scale. Curious if you’ve tried working with the native PO system yet where does it fall short the most in your workflow? kthoppae May 5, 2026, 4:45am 18 I think this is where it gets tricky. Even if another tool can create POs, the harder part is keeping everything connected across purchasing, receiving, and reporting. Once that flow gets split between systems, it tends to add more manual work and reconciliation. Curious how others are thinking about this going into the sunset are you trying to keep it in one place, or accepting some level of split? Philip_Rose July 8, 2026, 12:58am 20 Coming at this from the developer side, so take it with that context: the reason nothing has fully replaced the “print from a confirmed PO” flow is structural, there’s still no Purchase Order API, so apps simply can’t see PO data at all. There’s nothing to build on yet. On the “keep it in one place vs accept a split” question above: honestly, until a PO endpoint ships, some split is unavoidable, every workaround that exists routes around the PO object rather than through it. Two approaches are out in the wild: apps that hook into the native Transfers page (works if your stock movements live in Transfers), and apps that take a pasted list / CSV of what actually arrived (works wherever your PO lives — supplier spreadsheet, emailed packing list, another system). Neither needs the missing API, which is the point. And on where native POs fall short most, from what I’ve seen with migrating retailers, it’s the receiving end. Ordered is received — partial deliveries are the norm — and the moment stock lands you need labels printed for what’s actually in the box. That whole step just isn’t in the native flow. If Shopify does ship a PO API later, these workarounds can presumably plug into it. But with the August cut off, I wouldn’t plan a migration around waiting for it. MyWorks July 8, 2026, 1:22am 21 We decided not to wait around, and fueled by both our frustration with Stocky’s shortcomings, and our own users asking us for a robust way to handle POs with Shopify; decided to build our own solution. Check it out at Stockroom - Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Unlimited purchase orders, receiving & sync with QuickBooks | Shopify App Store - we’re making it completely free for everyone. We think Shopify merchants deserve a robust, stable and long term way to handle Purchase Orders in a way that fits their business. lspoor94 July 8, 2026, 9:20am 22 So with Shopify’s DotDev event happening in a couple weeks, there are numerous talks, including one specific: The Physical Ledger: Inventory gets GraphQL APIs Real world inventory is messy. We’re bringing it natively into Admin with new GraphQL primitives for purchase orders, stateful counts, and bins. Come see the schemas and build high-scale warehouse integrations. So it sounds like we will be getting an API for purchase orders (amongst other things too). Philip_Rose July 9, 2026, 9:32pm 23 Well that answers the thread’s original question in two ways at once. The DotDev sessions description (“GraphQL primitives for purchase orders, stateful counts, and bins”) is the first concrete sign of a PO API. This is surely good news for everyone building around this gap, since every work around discussed above can plug into it, once it ships. One timing caveat worth stating plainly: a conference session in a couple of weeks means schemas and previews, not a GA API — anyone migrating off Stocky before 31 August still shouldn’t plan around waiting for it. By the way, congratulations to MyWorks on shipping Stockroom — a free PO + receiving flow with label printing built in is a strong answer for stores that want the whole lifecycle in one place. After this thread’s developments, the remaining gap cases are narrower but real: deliveries whose paperwork never enters a PO system at all (supplier spreadsheets, emailed packing notes), and stores that need more control over the labels themselves — custom sizes, layouts, roll printers. That’s where the label-first tools still earn their keep. Between an API on the horizon, free PO apps, and the label apps, the post-Stocky picture finally looks less scary than it did in February. title: Csv download from the new PO's creation, replacing stocky? It was a quick and easy way to create barcoded labels for all received stock items
text: Csv download from the new PO's creation, replacing stocky? It was a quick and easy way to create barcoded labels for all received stock items = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Csv download from the new PO's creation, replacing stocky? It was a quick and easy way to create barcoded labels for all received stock items Technical Q&A customizations AI-generated summary Merchants are looking for a replacement workflow for Stocky’s CSV export used to print barcode labels for newly received inventory in Shopify POS locations. The main gap identified is that Shopify’s native Purchase Orders do not currently provide a clean CSV of only the items actually received, which matters especially for partial deliveries. Key points raised: A full PO export can overprint labels because it reflects ordered quantities, not received quantities. The preferred data source should be the receipt, transfer, or shipment lines showing what arrived. Essential CSV fields suggested include barcode, product title, variant, retail price, and quantity received; barcodes should be treated as text to preserve leading zeros. Several workaround paths were proposed, including exporting inventory data, using supplier packing-list CSVs, or adopting third-party apps that support PO receiving, Stocky migration, barcode check-in, direct label printing, or CSV/PDF/Dymo/Zebra output. No native Shopify solution or confirmed CSV feature was announced. The issue remains open, with the practical resolution being third-party tools or manual export workflows for now. PBN1 June 10, 2026, 5:45pm 1 Since Stocky is going away will there be a way to get a csv download of received items in the new PO creation link under Products. Stocky is currently the only quick way to create barcode labels for incoming stock for POS locations. Pipokx June 10, 2026, 7:04pm 2 Hey @PBN1 , Indeed, there is a major operational gap right now when it comes to barcode printing workflow. To figure out the cleanest way to extract and route that data for you, I’d look into two things: Your Printing Setup: Once you have the CSV of received items, what software or hardware are you using to actually generate the labels (e.g., Dymo, Zebra, Shopify’s Retail Barcode app)? Partial Deliveries: If a PO is only partially delivered, do you need the CSV to strictly isolate the newly received units, or the entire original PO? Curious to hear how you are handling the transition! Thanks, Julien Clement_Foltzer June 25, 2026, 7:20am 4 Disclosure up front: I build LabelCraft. The CSV export-then-reimport dance is exactly the gap Stocky left. LabelCraft reads a received Transfer or Shipment directly and prints exact-size labels for every line item, so there’s no CSV step at all. It also prints from a pasted or uploaded SKU list if you’d rather skip Transfers, and generates a valid GS1/EAN-13 for anything missing a barcode so it scans at the till. Free up to 200 labels a month if you want to try it on your next received batch. Whatever you land on, export your Stocky data before Aug 31, it doesn’t migrate automatically. MyWorks July 9, 2026, 9:49pm 5 If it helps, we do support label printing in the PO app we recently built - completely free, to help merchants as Stocky goes away. Check it out at Stockroom - Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Unlimited purchase orders, receiving & sync with QuickBooks | Shopify App Store - we’re making it completely free for everyone. We think Shopify merchants deserve a robust, stable and long term way to handle Purchase Orders in a way that fits their business. DougInOr July 12, 2026, 5:00pm 7 I don’t think a CSV output will happen under the native POs. You can though either utilize Stocky’s API, download those POs into a CSV now using Stocky’s download feature (pain the the …) or just move to an app that has a migration from Stocky using their API. Using an app that does have a Stocky API integration (like FyreTrail ’s Stocky Migration Tool), you can download your delivered POs, your incoming POs, Suppliers and Adjustments into FyreTrail and then print labels directly from the PO for items that you receive. There’s a ton of flexibility to get your data out of Stocky and into FyreTrail in plenty of time and you can simply pick up where you left off (many stores who use FyreTrail have done just that). If you choose to do that you will get a solid replacement in FyreTrail that has more intelligence built in to the day to day operations that you previously did in Stocky. If you just want to print labels then the 2 other apps (LabelCraft and FlochForster) are likely great solutions for you as well. Clement_Foltzer July 12, 2026, 7:25pm 8 Quick follow-up since this thread picked back up (still the LabelCraft founder). @FlochForster puts a finger on the real pain: partial deliveries. Exporting the whole PO gives you labels for the ordered quantities, not for what actually arrived. That is exactly why we read the received lines of a native Transfer or Shipment instead of the PO: one label per unit actually received in this delivery, nothing else. @PBN1 if you already have a Stocky CSV and want to sanity-check what will print before touching anything: we put a free, no-install checker at labelcraft.tech/stocky-label-preview. Paste the CSV, it previews the labels and flags missing or non-scannable barcodes. No account needed. On the Stocky API route @DougInOr mentions: agreed, that is the clean path for PO history. For the label half specifically you do not need history, just the received lines going forward. haloxzk July 20, 2026, 3:57am 9 Hi @PBN1 - I am researching the receiving-to-label workflow after Stocky, not promoting an app. I tested Shopify Transfers and found that basic received-quantity label printing is already covered, so I am trying to understand the remaining CSV gap. For your most recent delivery, did the CSV need to come from Shopify’s native PO, or would a supplier packing-list CSV have worked? Which exception took the most time: a partial receipt, a SKU mismatch, or a missing barcode? If you are comfortable sharing only an anonymized header row or 5-20 rows with fake values, I can turn it into a no-cost reconciliation mockup and send the result back for feedback. kingstore August 23, 2026, 4:15am 10 @PBN1 Native Purchase Orders still do not give you a clean CSV of what you just received so you can print barcode labels the way Stocky did. That gap is real. Workarounds people use: Export inventory (or the products you care about) and feed your label software from that, not from the PO receive screen. On partial deliveries, filter to what actually arrived or use a tool that treats each receipt as its own label batch. A full PO export labels ordered qty, not received qty. Some label apps pull barcodes from Shopify products without Stocky. If your flow is receive on the floor then print labels for what hit the shelf, a warehouse app that does scan receive plus labels in one pass is usually less painful than CSV glue. I work on SKUSavvy which handles barcode check-in and labels as part of the floor workflow (plus bin put-away if you need it). Happy to answer ops questions for anyone stuck on the Stocky label gap. vishalkundar September 3, 2026, 5:54pm 11 If the main reason you need the CSV is to print labels after receiving, Replenly can skip that extra step. It handles PO receiving, including partial receiving, and lets you print barcode labels for the PO directly. Free plan available, paid plans start at $19/month with a 14 day free trial. replenly.app Replenly — purchase orders and reorder forecasting for Shopify Know what to reorder today. Purchase orders, receiving, barcode stocktakes and Stocky CSV import, from $0. Denyslg September 5, 2026, 4:27am 12 Now that the thread has settled the CSV should come from what arrived rather than what you ordered, the columns decide whether it prints. Five of them. Barcode, exactly as it sits on the variant and formatted as text, or Excel eats the leading zeros. Product title, and the variant in its own column, because “Blue / M” glued onto a long title wraps and ruins the alignment on a small label. Retail price, since a label without one sends staff back to a screen. Quantity received, which is how many labels to print, not how many you ordered. Then the format question. A Dymo or Zebra path sends each label at true size as you receive, one line at a time. A PDF sheet suits labelling a whole delivery at a bench, and fails the day a driver scales it to 96 percent and scanners start rejecting the quiet zones. text: Print Barcode Labels from Purchase Orders = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Print Barcode Labels from Purchase Orders - Anyone else? Shopify Discussion product-feedback , inventory-management , barcode , troubleshooting AI-generated summary Merchants want Shopify to support native barcode label printing directly from Purchase Orders, especially for the exact quantities received, to avoid duplicate work during receiving and improve inventory accuracy. The main technical issue discussed is Shopify’s API access. Several replies note that native Purchase Orders are not exposed through Shopify’s Admin API, so third-party apps generally cannot read the PO document itself or add a true PO-based print workflow inside Shopify. Recent updates add an important workaround: if a Shopify PO is linked to a Transfer, receiving happens through an InventoryShipment, which is API-readable. One app builder reports testing this end to end and seeing received quantities such as acceptedQuantity=6, meaning apps may be able to print labels from the actual shipment/receipt without CSV re-entry. Other current options include CSV imports, receiving through Transfers, or using third-party inventory/label apps. Key buying criteria raised were whether tools print from received rather than ordered quantities, handle partial deliveries, flag missing barcodes/SKUs, and avoid data drifting from Shopify. No native Shopify solution was announced; the issue remains open, with app-based workarounds available. Wildernest1 June 19, 2026, 8:28pm 1 Is anyone else interested in being able to print barcode labels natively within Shopify Purchase Orders? The recent purchase order updates have been a great improvement, but this feels like one important missing piece. Being able to print barcode labels directly from the exact quantities received on a PO would make inventory management significantly more efficient and help improve inventory accuracy. From a workflow perspective, this seems like a relatively straightforward feature to implement, and it would add a lot of value for retailers who rely on accurate receiving and tagging. Would love to see this included in a future update. MDS73 June 26, 2026, 1:27pm 3 I don’t understand why this problem isn’t at the top of the list. Every merchant would love to print labels and barcodes directly from a PO, without making the same job twice. Hope anybody here could help us about it. DougInOr June 26, 2026, 5:27pm 4 This is the benefit of custom apps that people often look at and frown on due to the extra expense. Custom apps give you the “nice to have” features that Shopify may not have as a high priority against their wall of prioritized items. Custom apps are focused and cater very closely to what their subscribers want. FlochForster July 11, 2026, 6:12am 6 Following up, it’s live on the App Store now, free tier (200 labels/mo) needs no card: apps.shopify.com FlochLabels - Print barcode labels from transfers, purchase orders, and CSVs... Print retail barcode labels from Shopify transfers, purchase orders, or CSV. Quantities pre-fill from what you received; missing barcodes get valid EAN-13s. If anyone tries a receiving day and labels don’t line up, reply or DM and I’ll help you set up. Clement_Foltzer July 19, 2026, 4:32pm 8 There are two workable paths today, depending on where you receive stock. If you can receive through native Transfers instead of (or alongside) POs: Transfers are exposed through Shopify’s API, so an app can read the exact received quantities directly and print from them, nothing re-entered. Native Purchase Orders are the opposite case: Shopify does not expose them via API, so no app can read them at all, which is precisely why this feels like doing the same job twice. If you have to stay on POs, the realistic workaround is CSV: get the PO line items into a file (SKU, barcode, quantity received), either exported or built from the supplier’s packing list, and print labels from that. Not elegant, but it keeps quantities exact and avoids manual cross-referencing. Agree with @DougInOr that a third-party app is the practical route for now. Whatever you evaluate, the thing to test is whether it accepts received quantities from a Transfer or a CSV, rather than making you pick products one by one, since that is where the double work creeps back in. FYI I built LabelCraft, a barcode label app that works from both of those inputs. Custom-Cursor July 19, 2026, 4:52pm 9 Hey @Wildernest1 , hope you are doing well! I agree native barcode label printing from Purchase Orders would make the receiving workflow much more efficient and improve inventory accuracy. YoBeCo August 13, 2026, 11:09pm 10 Adding to this, based on testing it hands-on this week. Native POs aren’t readable directly, that part is right, there’s no PurchaseOrder object in the Admin API. But merchants on the native PO flow aren’t stuck, because the PO flow has no independent receiving. When you create a PO in the admin and link a transfer, Shopify auto-creates the shipment once it goes in transit, and you receive against that. So the receive event lands on an InventoryShipment either way. I tested this end to end: created a PO, linked the transfer, received 6 of 10 through the admin flow. The API showed acceptedQuantity=6 on the line, and origin.name came back as the supplier name from the PO. So an app can show “delivery from [supplier]” and print exact received quantities with no CSV step, even for merchants who only ever think in POs. Worth knowing if you’re evaluating tools: the question isn’t really whether it supports POs, it’s whether it reads the shipment the PO produced. Disclosure: I’m building in this space too (LabelDock, in review right now). Philip_Rose August 15, 2026, 1:35am 11 Late addition, with the same disclosure as the others in this thread — I build in this space too ( LabelLoom , on the App Store). The InventoryShipment finding above is genuinely useful — if your POs live in Shopify and you receive through the linked transfer, that path has you covered, and it’s good news the received quantities turn out to be readable after all. The case I built for is the one that never touches Shopify at all: the delivery that arrives with a supplier spreadsheet or a paper packing note — no PO or transfer in the admin anywhere. You paste or CSV-import the list (SKUs + quantities, partial deliveries fine), it matches your catalogue, loudly flags anything it can’t find instead of silently dropping it, and prints to Dymo/Zebra/Avery presets scan-tested on the physical printers. It’ll also generate barcodes for products that don’t have one yet, without ever overwriting existing ones. Until Stocky switches off on 31 August every label is free — the meter only starts in September — so it costs nothing to test whichever tool matches where your deliveries actually live. Lillianruan August 21, 2026, 4:51am 12 Definitely. Barcode labels at receiving make a huge difference once you’re handling more inventory. If you don’t want to wait for Shopify to add it natively, have a look at Lofko. It’s built more around the inventory/warehouse side of the workflow, so receiving, barcodes and stock management can all sit in the same process. kingstore August 23, 2026, 1:48am 13 Yes this would certainly help many stores who need labels as they go. Likely this will come with time. Shopifys own label printer does let you print off a list of barcodes for SKUs so what you could do is export the PO, then use this as a starting place to ‘import the SKUs’ into the Retail Barcode Labels - Create and print barcode labels for your products | Shopify App Store What you’d want to do in this case, for large POs at least is tag the items in the PO, then use that tag to determine which products need to be printed. Alternatively, you can use an app like SKUSavvy AI Powered WMS - AI powered mobile WMS to streamline inventory and ship faster | Shopify App Store which has native printing directly from the PO put-away enabling you to select all, counted quantities, received quantities, or individual. skusavvy-print-po-items 2804×1860 285 KB Hope that helps! jmiralles August 24, 2026, 7:34am 14 he reason none of the apps here can print from your Shopify PO is that purchase orders aren’t exposed in the Admin API. An app can read products, variants and inventory, but not the PO you created in the admin. So every tool in this thread works the same way: the PO lives in the app, and the labels come from there. Two things worth checking before you pick one, because that’s where the duplicate work actually comes from: 1. Does it print from received quantities or ordered ones? If 40 of 100 arrive, you want 40 labels, not 100 — otherwise you’re re-counting by hand anyway, which is the thing you were trying to avoid. 2. Does it fall back to the SKU when a variant has no barcode? Most catalogues have a few, and a silently skipped label is worse than a wrong one: you find out at the shelf. Disclosure: I build EasyRestock, which works that way — one label per unit received, or per unit ordered if nothing has been received yet, on A4 sheets or 57×32 rolls. Same trade-off as everyone else here: the PO lives in the app, not in Shopify’s own PO screen. YoBeCo August 25, 2026, 2:46pm 15 Following up on my post above, since Stocky goes off this week. On the point just above about every tool working the same way, with the PO living in the app: the first half is right, there’s no PurchaseOrder object in the Admin API, so nothing can read the PO document itself. But that isn’t the only way out, and there’s a third path that needs no re-entry and no CSV. When you create a PO in the Shopify admin and link a transfer, Shopify auto-creates a shipment once that transfer goes in transit, and receiving happens against that shipment. The shipment is exposed through the API, and its line items carry the accepted, rejected and unreceived quantities, with the supplier name on the transfer origin. I tested it end to end: received 6 of 10 through the normal admin flow, and the API returned acceptedQuantity=6 with origin.name set to the supplier from the PO. So you can keep creating purchase orders exactly where you do today, in Shopify, and still print labels for what actually arrived. The app reads the shipment your PO produced, rather than a second copy of the PO kept somewhere else. Disclosure, same as everyone else here: I build LabelDock, which went live on the App Store today. MyWorks August 25, 2026, 6:22pm 16 Feel free to give Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Purchase orders, inventory management, reporting, COGS + more | Shopify App Store a try? We’ve built it completely free for Shopify merchants; and it includes quite a bit of functionality around barcodes and labels - both in terms of supporting barcode scanners, as well as label printing! You can customize how you want the label to look, and easily print from products, POs, and more. juhyun_han September 14, 2026, 1:04am 17 @Wildernest1 @MDS73 — @Clement_Foltzer ’s point is the structural one: Transfers are in the Admin API and native purchase orders are not, so the PO screen cannot get a print button from a third party no matter who builds it. Worth adding what that means for anything you do buy, and one trap in the workflow itself that decides whether the labels are any use. Print from what arrived, not from what was ordered. Almost every version of this prints the PO line quantity, because that is the number on the screen when you raise the order. Partial deliveries then break it. Twelve ordered, five turn up, you print twelve labels — seven loose labels now exist for stock that is not in the building. They get used on the next delivery, which is the right product at the wrong cost, or they go in a drawer and somebody sticks them on in six weeks. The label has to come off the receipt event, per line, at the quantity actually counted in. Two consequences of that worth checking before you pay for anything: Does it label the partial, and can it label the remainder later? A receiving workflow that only prints once per PO is unusable for anyone whose supplier short-ships, which is everyone. Which cost does the label’s row carry? If the app prints from the ordered cost and the invoice arrives above the order — a supplier raising a price between quote and delivery is routine and nobody is told — the barcode scans fine while your cost record is wrong. That error is invisible until you look at margin a month later and cannot explain it. And the caution about the API gap, since it is the thing that will surprise you: because native POs are not exposed, any app that does this keeps its own purchase orders rather than reading yours. That is not a flaw, it is the only option available — but it means your PO history then lives in two places, and the app’s view of what has been received can drift from Shopify’s inventory if anyone adjusts stock outside it. Before buying, the question I would ask is what happens when the two disagree, and whether the app can tell you that they do. Disclosure: I build an inventory app with its own purchase orders, so I have an interest and the above describes a limitation of my own design as much as anyone’s. @FlochForster ’s app already covers the transfers-and-CSV route with a free tier, which is the path that actually works today. text: Trying to weed through the suggestions for a Stocky replacement = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Trying to weed through the suggestions for a Stocky replacement Shopify Apps inventory-management REBRecords June 23, 2026, 9:06pm 1 I’ve been reading through the various posts and looking at the suggested apps to replace Stocky and can’t seem to settle on one. I’m hoping that by posting what we need to be able to do the community can help me narrow it down! PO generation: We use Stocky to generate POs based on sales trends and current inventory (usually no more than 10/week). Additionally, we add as many as 40 new SKUs to our inventory each week (which is quite time consuming). Receive POs: Often between ordering and receiving items go on backorder from the supplier and so we rarely receive a complete PO in one shipment. Usually we are receiving from as many as 3-6 POs in a given shipment (sometimes more). I’ve noticed that many apps allow barcode scanning for receiving orders, this would be a welcome addition! Print barcode labels: When we receive an entire (or at least a large portion of a) PO this has been fairly easy to do via CSV files and the Dymo app. Retail Barcode Labels is what we currently use to print individual labels. Thanks in advance! I’m looking forward to your input. Jason REB Records DougInOr June 23, 2026, 9:51pm 2 Hi Jason… Did you look at FyreTrail yet? I don’t recognize that you have yet so you should go take a look at us as well. Here’s why: PO Generation: You can add products based on sales trends (also seasonality and event/holiday pressure) for various horizon lengths of time (30, 60, 90, 180 days). It’s the SKU adding that will make things the easiest though because of how FyreTrail works. It’s geared around only what product details you need to enter, but also when you need to enter them and how FyreTrail does a lot of it for you that saves the time. Receiving POs: Partial receiving is done well from FyreTrail. You can have multiple receivings for a single order. Barcode scanning is included in the ways to receive orders. Printing Barcode Labels: FyreTrail allows you to print ONLY what has been delivered for an order. In other words, if you receive the full order, FyreTrail will allow you to print the quantities of labels needed for each product on that order. Receiving a partial order means FyreTrail only prints what has actually been delivered. Some other things you may find helpful - you can also do the following during this process too: Set Min/Max Levels: you can set these levels on a product or variant then create a PO from Low Stock to Target Stock. Create Custom Label Templates: Having one type of label or many, you can create a custom label for one or more printer types - how you want it. Can’t quite get what you want? Reach out and I’ll generally be able to make it for you. POS Delivery: You can receive POs directly from the POS with our Tile Extension. Add the tile, press the tile, enter the order number, brand or product then pick the right order and start the receiving process right from the POS. There’s a ton more like stock takes, adjustments, transfers, budgeting etc. too. Hope to see you soon! PS: Forgot to add, we’ve also added a Stocky Migration Tool that will help you bring your items over to FyreTrail (where Stocky allows anyway) to make any transition as easy as it can be. Clement_Foltzer June 25, 2026, 7:19am 4 Disclosure: I built LabelCraft, so factor that in. Of your three needs it only covers the third (printing labels), so it isn’t a full Stocky replacement on its own. But for that piece: point it at a received Transfer, or paste/upload your received SKU list, and it bulk-prints exact-size Dymo labels, default quantity zero so you never short a roll, and generates a valid GS1/EAN-13 for anything missing a barcode. Most people pair it with a lightweight PO tool for the ordering side. Free up to 200 labels a month. Either way, export your Stocky data before Aug 31, it doesn’t auto-migrate. REBRecords June 25, 2026, 6:31pm 5 Thank you for the thorough reply! This is one of the apps I have looked at and your information is a big help in understanding what the app actually does. DougInOr June 25, 2026, 6:37pm 6 Of course! Do let me know if there’s anything else you needed to know. Otherwise - see you in FyreTrail! SectionKit June 25, 2026, 9:39pm 7 Hi @REBRecords . Inventory Planner is the best fit, but its pricy. Stock&Buy is more affordable and has PO generation, partial shipment receiving, and barcode labels. Keep you curent Retail Barcode Labels setup regardless of which app you choose. lspoor94 June 27, 2026, 10:53am 8 Stockful could potentially be a good fit, it’s built directly in the admin and no external dashboard. The only thing really missing is PO’s, but with Shopify connecting PO’s to Inventory Transfers now, it isn’t too bad and Stockful does read off inventory transfers. apps.shopify.com Stockful: Inventory Management - AI inventory assistant: forecasts, stock... AI inventory assistant: track stock at every location, get demand forecasts, sell-through analytics, 12 report types, and Slack low-stock alerts. MyWorks July 9, 2026, 10:52pm 9 @REBRecords If it helps; just wanted to add a comment here. With Stocky going away, and our own users asking us for a robust way to handle POs and light inventory management / reordering with Shopify; we decided to build our own solution, but for free.
