text: Advice on bar code scanners and the best app = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Advice on bar code scanners and the best app Shopify Apps troubleshooting AI-generated summary A Shopify merchant with about 300 products and two stock locations asked how to use EAN barcodes, scanners, and label printing to reduce missing stock and inventory mismatches. Recommendations centered on combining hardware with a disciplined stock workflow. Suggested hardware included wireless/Bluetooth scanners such as Socket Mobile or Zebra models, basic USB/Bluetooth 2D scanners, phone-camera scanning as a lower-cost start, and thermal label printers such as Zebra ZD410 or Rollo. For apps, several options were proposed: FyreTrail for inventory counting and location tracking, EasyScan for scanning during order packing, SkuVault for stronger multi-location inventory, Binly for scan counts and variance reports, and Easify Inventory Sync for syncing inventory across stores or channels. Stocky was mentioned, but another reply warned it is being sunset on August 31. The main advice was to track every stock movement: receiving, transfers between locations, shelf/bin placement, picking, packing, and regular cycle counts. The original poster thanked contributors, but no final implementation results were shared; a later request for before/after feedback remains unanswered. Mungo2007 April 8, 2026, 12:25pm 1 Hi All I need some advice for our online store. We have recently set up EAN codes for all of our products about 300 active products so now we want to use a barcode scanner system for the stock, orders out, just to keep a better track of the inventory as we are having problems with losing stock and where it is located and the system showing stock when we don’t actually have it. I am looking for advice on the best app to use and any advice you can give for barcode scanners we have 2 stock locations so i guess we will need a battery type scanner with a memory function. I will also need a barcode label printer for the products. So anyone that has experience of this your advice would be hugely helpful DougInOr April 8, 2026, 1:57pm 2 FyreTrail can help you with this. FyreTrail offers inventory tracking as far as how many you have in stock, how many you have sold and allows you to put low inventory limits and target inventory limits on every item you have in your store allowing you to easily create new purchase orders to replenish low stock. Purchase orders are tracked based on date, supplier, quantity so you always know what you have coming in at any point in time as well. Ok, so that’s that, but then you want to scan inventory and track how many you actually have in your physical store too. FyreTrail handles that for you as well by allowing you to create inventory counting “sessions” where you and your team can tackle sections of your store or warehouse and count your items that you actually have. This is compared by what Shopify says you have in stock and you can update those values accordingly. All of this is organized by location not only by what locations you have defined in Shopify, but also by your location definitions that you create (“Section 5” or “Mid-Shelf” or “Area B”, etc.). In the next few weeks we are releasing some new features in these areas that should help you better target your inventory with cycle counting capabilities and product searching that will help you identify when an item was last scanned, where it was last scanned at, etc. I think FyreTrail offers everything you’re asking for here. ShopIntegrations April 8, 2026, 8:17pm 3 For hardware, get a Zebra ZD410 or Rollo for printing labels. They’re absolute workhorses. For the scanner, the Socket Mobile S740 is the standard bluetooth scanner that integrates perfectly with Shopify and holds a charge all day. For software, it depends on your exact workflow. If you just want to receive stock and do cycle counts, Stocky (which is free if you use Shopify POS Pro) does the job. But if you want to scan items as you pack orders to stop shipping the wrong stuff, look at EasyScan. It’s pretty affordable and does exactly what you need for a 300 SKU catalog across a couple locations. DougInOr April 8, 2026, 8:33pm 4 I do not disagree, but be careful suggesting Stocky when it is sunsetting August 31st and will no longer be available. shopify-dev April 8, 2026, 8:54pm 5 Adding EAN codes barcode scanning will definitely help reduce stock errors. For Shopify, I’d recommend looking at apps like Stocky or inventory tools like SkuVault if you need stronger multi-location control. For scanners, go with a Bluetooth Zebra or socket mobile scanner. For label printing, a Zebra or Socket mobile scanner. Make sure the app supports multi-location inventory + stock transfers to avoid mismatches. Godspeed001 April 9, 2026, 12:59am 6 Hi, Implementing EAN codes and introducing barcode-based stock control is definitely the right step, especially with 300 active products and multiple stock locations . From what you’ve described, the main issue is likely not just the lack of scanners, but the absence of a consistent stock movement process . A barcode system can solve a lot of this, but only if it’s set up to track stock properly at every stage. What you should be looking for You’ll want a setup that covers three areas : 1) Inventory / barcode management app Choose an app that can handle: barcode scanning stock counts stock transfers between locations order picking / packing inventory adjustments ideally bin or shelf location tracking That last part is important, because if products are physically in the wrong place, Shopify can still show stock even when your team can’t actually find it. 2) Wireless barcode scanners For your setup, I would strongly recommend: wireless / battery-powered scanners ideally with memory / batch mode That way, staff can scan products while walking around the warehouse or between locations, then sync later if needed. This is especially useful for: stock takes receiving deliveries moving stock between locations picking orders 3) Thermal barcode label printer A thermal label printer is the best option for product labels and shelf labels because they are: faster cleaner more reliable better for regular warehouse use The real fix: improve the stock workflow This is the part that usually solves the problem. Even with the best app and hardware, stock issues will continue unless every movement is tracked consistently. Recommended workflow When stock comes in: Scan every product in Assign it to the correct stock location If possible, assign it to a specific shelf/bin When stock is moved: Always scan it out of one location Then scan it into the other location When orders are being fulfilled: Scan products during picking Scan again during packing This helps prevent dispatch mistakes and catches missing items before the order leaves. Ongoing stock control: Run regular cycle counts instead of waiting for a full stock take For example, count part of the inventory weekly instead of everything at once every few months That usually makes a huge difference in keeping stock accurate. Best type of setup for your situation With 300 products and 2 locations , I would personally focus on a system that includes: a barcode inventory app that supports multi-location stock 2 wireless scanners 1 thermal label printer clear bin / shelf labelling a strict rule that nothing moves without being scanned That’s what will actually stop stock from “disappearing” or showing in the system when it’s not physically there. One important tip before you buy anything Before choosing an app or hardware, I’d make sure it can do all of the following: work properly with Shopify multi-location inventory support stock transfers support stock counts support order picking / packing work with your chosen scanner and label printer A lot of apps sound good at first, but only handle one part of the process. In short If your goal is to fix stock accuracy and improve order handling, I’d recommend building a setup around: barcode scanning location-based stock tracking thermal label printing and most importantly, a disciplined scanning process for every stock movement That combination will give you much better control over: missing stock inaccurate inventory stock sitting in the wrong location dispatch errors products showing as available when they aren’t actually there Mungo2007 April 9, 2026, 12:47pm 8 Thank you for all the great replies this really helps me with the guidance you have given DavisHTChang September 6, 2026, 2:31am 9 @Mungo2007 curious how this turned out — did the barcode scanner + label printer setup fix the “system shows stock we don’t actually have” problem across your two locations, or did the mismatches keep creeping back (e.g. after transfers or returns)? I’m looking at the same gap for a few other two-location stores, so any before/after you can share would be genuinely useful. Denyslg September 16, 2026, 3:44am 10 For the scanner, hardware barely matters at 300 products. A basic USB or Bluetooth 2D scanner works like a keyboard, so most inventory apps read it fine, and you can even count from a phone camera first if you would rather not buy hardware yet. The label printer is separate, a Zebra or similar thermal printer works with most apps that generate barcode labels. On tracking, since stock is going missing across two locations, turn on Shopify’s native inventory transfer feature, it keeps a record whenever stock physically moves between them, worth doing before you add an app. A manual count against that log in a spreadsheet catches a good chunk of the drift on its own. I build Binly, so take that into account, but scanning a section or the whole shop by phone camera or USB scanner, with a variance report before anything applies, is built for exactly this kind of stock going missing. apps.shopify.com Binly ‑ Stocktake & Reorder - Stocky replacement: phone stocktakes, POs &... Stocky shuts down Aug 31, 2026. Binly replaces it for $19/mo: phone barcode stocktakes, purchase orders, smart reorder, free white-glove migration. Easify-Jennifer September 17, 2026, 2:33am 11 Hi @Mungo2007 It sounds like you’ve already taken a great first step by assigning EAN codes to all of your products. From what you’re describing, I’d focus not only on the scanner itself, but also on building a workflow where every stock movement is scanned consistently. In my experience, that’s usually what makes the biggest difference in reducing inventory discrepancies. For hardware, many merchants use wireless Bluetooth barcode scanners with rechargeable batteries, especially when working across multiple stock locations. A scanner with offline storage/memory can be useful if you’re scanning away from a workstation and syncing data later. For label printing, thermal label printers are generally a popular choice since they don’t require ink and are well-suited for printing barcode labels in bulk. On the software side, I’d suggest looking at inventory solutions that support barcode-based receiving, stock counts, transfers between locations, and order fulfillment. Since you have two stock locations, the ability to track inventory movements between locations will likely be just as important as the barcode scanning itself. A few best practices that have helped many merchants improve inventory accuracy are: Assigning bin/shelf locations to products. Scanning products when receiving stock and fulfilling orders. Performing regular cycle counts instead of waiting for a full annual stocktake. Recording transfers between locations rather than adjusting inventory manually. If you’re also selling through multiple stores or sales channels and need inventory to stay synchronized between them, a solution like Easify Inventory Sync may be worth exploring alongside your barcode workflow. While it doesn’t replace warehouse scanning software, it can help keep inventory quantities aligned across connected products and channels, which can reduce overselling and stock mismatches. I’d be interested to know a bit more about your setup—are you running everything through Shopify only, or do you also sell through marketplaces, POS, or additional Shopify stores? That can make a big difference when choosing the right inventory system. Related topics Topic Replies Views Activity Where to find a compatible barcode scanner for my app? text: Allow barcode label printing directly from a Purchase Order or Transfer number = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Allow barcode label printing directly from a Purchase Order or Transfer number Shopify Discussion troubleshooting AI-generated summary Retailers are requesting a native way for Shopify’s Retail Barcode Labels app to create label batches directly from received inventory in a Purchase Order (PO) or Transfer, instead of manually adding each product/variant again after receiving stock. Key requirements raised: Label quantities should default to the actually received/accepted quantity, not the original ordered quantity, to avoid over-printing during partial shipments. Ideally labels should be tied to a specific receipt or shipment so users can reprint that delivery later without rebuilding the list. The workflow should flag missing or duplicate barcodes before printing, especially for new products arriving on their first PO. Several app developers noted workarounds or third-party implementations, including building batches from received transfer shipments, allowing editable counts, generating or flagging missing barcodes, and preventing duplicate barcode issues. One developer said Shopify’s native PO data is not exposed to apps via API, limiting direct integration with native POs; transfers or app-managed/imported POs are more feasible. No native Shopify solution has been confirmed. The request remains open, with upvoting and third-party workflows suggested as interim options. ginger_1 August 20, 2026, 8:47pm 1 Description: Currently, the Retail Barcode Labels app requires manually adding each product individually when printing labels — even after you’ve already received inventory against a Purchase Order or Transfer. This creates duplicate work in an otherwise streamlined receiving workflow. Requested improvement: Add the ability to enter a PO number or Transfer number in the Retail Barcode Labels app and have Shopify automatically pull in all line items and quantities from that PO or Transfer, ready to print. Why this matters: For retail stores receiving shipments regularly, this would eliminate a redundant manual step and reduce errors. The PO and Transfer data already exists in Shopify — connecting it to label printing is a natural extension of the receiving workflow. This process adds another whole step, and more opportunity for human error in the receiving process. Expected behavior: Search or select a PO or Transfer in the Retail Barcode Labels app All variants and quantities auto-populate Review and print in one step salor_works August 22, 2026, 6:48am 4 I’d definitely add one detail to this request: the label quantity should default to the actually received quantity , not the original ordered quantity. If a PO has 50 units but only 30 arrive in the first shipment, pulling the PO directly and printing 50 labels creates a new error while trying to remove manual work. Ideally the flow would be: PO / Transfer → select receipt → received variants + received quantities → review → print And then allow reprinting labels for that specific receipt later without rebuilding the list. Opsloft_Team August 22, 2026, 8:25am 5 One edge case worth folding into this request: new products often arrive on their very first PO before anyone has assigned them a barcode, so the auto-populate step should flag line items with missing or duplicate barcodes rather than quietly printing blank labels. Receiving is usually the moment people discover that, standing at the printer. The received-vs-ordered point above matters even more with partial shipments, since a 50-unit PO that arrives in two deliveries really needs two label runs tied to each receipt rather than one run against the PO total, which is a good argument for making the receipt, not the PO, the unit the label list is built from. SealSubs-Roan August 23, 2026, 5:38am 7 ginger_1: Description: Currently, the Retail Barcode Labels app requires manually adding each product individually when printing labels — even after you’ve already received inventory against a Purchase Order or Transfer. This creates duplicate work in an otherwise streamlined receiving workflow. Requested improvement: Add the ability to enter a PO number or Transfer number in the Retail Barcode Labels app and have Shopify automatically pull in all line items and quantities from that PO or Transfer, ready to print. Why this matters: For retail stores receiving shipments regularly, this would eliminate a redundant manual step and reduce errors. The PO and Transfer data already exists in Shopify — connecting it to label printing is a natural extension of the receiving workflow. This process adds another whole step, and more opportunity for human error in the receiving process. Expected behavior: Search or select a PO or Transfer in the Retail Barcode Labels app All variants and quantities auto-populate Review and print in one step Hi there @ginger_1 This would be a useful adds-on to the Retail Barcode Labels workflow. The variants and quantities received are already in the PO and Transfer, letting the user select one and pre-fill the label queue would be eliminating manual input which means errors. A practical workaround is to consider the received PO or Transfer as the source of truth and generate the label quantities based on the variants received. Native support for choosing a PO or Transfer would make this much quicker for stores that receive deliveries often. Clement_Foltzer August 31, 2026, 6:54am 8 Hi @ginger_1 On the request itself: there is no native way today to hand the Retail Barcode Labels app a PO or Transfer number and have it pull the lines in, so the manual re-entry you describe is the current reality. The request is a fair one and worth votes. On the two points raised in the replies, both matter more than they look. kai_xing and salor_works are right that the print quantity has to come from the received quantity, not the ordered quantity. Shopify’s shipment data exposes those as two separate fields, the accepted quantity per line and the ordered quantity, and a short or partial delivery is the common case rather than the edge case. Anything that prints off the ordered quantity will over-print on every partial delivery, and you tend to find out while holding the extra labels. Opsloft_Team’s point about products arriving on their first PO with no barcode yet is the other half of the problem. If you generate barcodes at receiving time, generate them before the label batch is built, and preview them before anything is written, because a barcode written onto a variant is painful to walk back once labels are already on stock. A practical interim workflow that does not wait on this feature request: receive the shipment natively, then drive the label batch off the shipment record rather than off a product list. That keeps the received quantity as the source of truth and it survives partial deliveries without any manual reconciliation. For transparency, that is what my app (LabelCraft) does. It reads native Transfers, builds the batch from the accepted quantity per line, and can generate and preview missing barcodes for products showing up on their first PO. I am not posting a link. The native feature you are asking for would still be the better answer for everyone, so I would keep pushing the request regardless. Denyslg September 1, 2026, 10:46pm 10 Disclosure first: I build Binly , an inventory app, so read this with that in mind. The reason nothing does this natively is buried in this thread already: Shopify’s API doesn’t expose purchase orders to apps. Nobody can read your native PO, so every real solution ends up being an app with its own PO flow. That said, the three problems raised here are exactly solvable, and worth demanding from whatever app you pick: Labels from received quantity, not ordered. salor_works nailed the danger — a PO for 50 where 30 arrived should give you 30 labels, not 50. Default to what was actually received. Editable counts before printing. Partial deliveries, damaged units, a box you’ll label tomorrow — you want to see every line with its count and adjust before anything prints. Missing barcodes caught before printing, like Opsloft_Team said. New products often have no barcode at all. The app should tell you “3 of 14 items have no barcode” and offer to generate valid EAN-13s for just those — never touching products that already have one. Binly does all three as of this week: receive a delivery on a PO, export a label file with one row per unit received (Dymo Connect prints one label per row), flip to ordered quantities when you want to prep labels before the truck arrives, adjust any line’s count, and generate barcodes for the items that lack them. Update, since things moved: it now also reads Shopify’s native transfer shipments — pick a shipment and the rows prefill from what you accepted at receiving. The native PO screen itself is still closed to every app (paragraph two), but the transfer your PO feeds is readable, and that covers the receiving flow this thread is about. Otherwise it works with POs created or imported in Binly — Stocky CSVs come across too. If you’re set on staying with native POs and the Retail Barcode Labels app, upvoting this thread is the right move. The API gap is Shopify’s to close. Tomer_Kaya September 3, 2026, 7:48pm 11 @ginger_1 I’m not with Shopify and I’m not selling anything, just trying to understand how retailers are handling this. You wrote that the Retail Barcode Labels app makes you add each product manually even after you’ve already received the inventory against a PO. How many items do you typically receive at once, and how long does the labelling take you today? Thanks. Rutus September 4, 2026, 5:02pm 12 The duplicate work you described caught my attention. If the PO or transfer already contains the products and quantities received, having to manually rebuild that same list again for labels seems like exactly the sort of repetitive step that should disappear. Out of curiosity, when you receive a larger shipment, roughly how many products/variants are you having to add manually before you can print the labels? little-darcy September 22, 2026, 8:40am 13 Did you get an Answer or Solution? I find it impossible to believe that this Shopify cant manage POs in a run of the mill way like other POS providers do. YoBeCo September 22, 2026, 7:40pm 14 Disclosure first: I build LabelDock, so read this with that in mind. On the question — nothing has changed that I can see. There is still no native path from a PO or a transfer to a label batch, and driving the labels off the received shipment rather than off a product list, as described above, is still the practical answer. Two things that have not come up in this thread. Duplicate barcodes, not just missing ones. There is a report from 15 September of new variants being created already carrying the main product’s barcode, so two variants of one product end up with the same code: BARCODE # for new variant being pre-filled with EXISTING barcode # (duplicate for all new variants) suddenly? — no Shopify reply on it yet, and one merchant there could not reproduce it, so treat it as a report rather than a rule. It is worth guarding against either way, because you do not find out at the printer, you find out at the till with the labels already on the stock. Flag any delivery where two lines share a barcode before anything prints. The second print on a delivery that arrives in rounds. A shipment received partially today and completed next week has its accepted quantity go from thirty to fifty. An app that simply prints the accepted quantity prints fifty the second time, on top of the thirty labels already on the stock. The second print should cover the twenty and nothing else. LabelDock does both, and it is read-only — it cannot write a barcode onto your products. Given how hard that is to walk back once labels are on stock, that is deliberate. Younes codeofsagar September 30, 2026, 1:13pm 15 (post deleted by author) codeofsagar September 30, 2026, 1:19pm 16 @kai_xing and @salor_work s are right, and specific enough that it is worth saying so concretely: we had this backwards. Disclosure first, I build ShelfSprint , a Shopify POS app for shelf refills. We shipped label printing from a purchase order last week, and it printed one label per unit still outstanding on the order. Receive 30 of 50 and you got 20 labels, for units that are not on the bench. Same error salor_works describes, pointing the other way. We changed it today to print per unit received. The part we cannot do yet is the flow salor_works actually asked for: pick a receipt, label that delivery, reprint that same receipt later without rebuilding the list. A purchase order line only carries a running received total, so “this delivery” is not a thing the data can answer until receipts are linked to orders. That is a real gap on our side, not a Shopify limitation. kai_xing’s interim control sheet is the right workaround in the meantime, for the reason given: reconciling total received against total labels catches the partial receipt before the labels are printed rather than after. text: Print Barcode Labels from Purchase Orders = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Print Barcode Labels from Purchase Orders - Anyone else? Shopify Discussion product-feedback , inventory-management , barcode , troubleshooting AI-generated summary Merchants want Shopify to support native barcode label printing directly from Purchase Orders, especially for the exact quantities received, to avoid duplicate work during receiving and improve inventory accuracy. The main technical issue discussed is Shopify’s API access. Several replies note that native Purchase Orders are not exposed through Shopify’s Admin API, so third-party apps generally cannot read the PO document itself or add a true PO-based print workflow inside Shopify. Recent updates add an important workaround: if a Shopify PO is linked to a Transfer, receiving happens through an InventoryShipment, which is API-readable. One app builder reports testing this end to end and seeing received quantities such as acceptedQuantity=6, meaning apps may be able to print labels from the actual shipment/receipt without CSV re-entry. Other current options include CSV imports, receiving through Transfers, or using third-party inventory/label apps. Key buying criteria raised were whether tools print from received rather than ordered quantities, handle partial deliveries, flag missing barcodes/SKUs, and avoid data drifting from Shopify. No native Shopify solution was announced; the issue remains open, with app-based workarounds available. Wildernest1 June 19, 2026, 8:28pm 1 Is anyone else interested in being able to print barcode labels natively within Shopify Purchase Orders? The recent purchase order updates have been a great improvement, but this feels like one important missing piece. Being able to print barcode labels directly from the exact quantities received on a PO would make inventory management significantly more efficient and help improve inventory accuracy. From a workflow perspective, this seems like a relatively straightforward feature to implement, and it would add a lot of value for retailers who rely on accurate receiving and tagging. Would love to see this included in a future update. MDS73 June 26, 2026, 1:27pm 3 I don’t understand why this problem isn’t at the top of the list. Every merchant would love to print labels and barcodes directly from a PO, without making the same job twice. Hope anybody here could help us about it. DougInOr June 26, 2026, 5:27pm 4 This is the benefit of custom apps that people often look at and frown on due to the extra expense. Custom apps give you the “nice to have” features that Shopify may not have as a high priority against their wall of prioritized items. Custom apps are focused and cater very closely to what their subscribers want. FlochForster July 11, 2026, 6:12am 6 Following up, it’s live on the App Store now, free tier (200 labels/mo) needs no card: apps.shopify.com FlochLabels - Print barcode labels from transfers, purchase orders, and CSVs... Print retail barcode labels from Shopify transfers, purchase orders, or CSV. Quantities pre-fill from what you received; missing barcodes get valid EAN-13s. If anyone tries a receiving day and labels don’t line up, reply or DM and I’ll help you set up. Clement_Foltzer July 19, 2026, 4:32pm 8 There are two workable paths today, depending on where you receive stock. If you can receive through native Transfers instead of (or alongside) POs: Transfers are exposed through Shopify’s API, so an app can read the exact received quantities directly and print from them, nothing re-entered. Native Purchase Orders are the opposite case: Shopify does not expose them via API, so no app can read them at all, which is precisely why this feels like doing the same job twice. If you have to stay on POs, the realistic workaround is CSV: get the PO line items into a file (SKU, barcode, quantity received), either exported or built from the supplier’s packing list, and print labels from that. Not elegant, but it keeps quantities exact and avoids manual cross-referencing. Agree with @DougInOr that a third-party app is the practical route for now. Whatever you evaluate, the thing to test is whether it accepts received quantities from a Transfer or a CSV, rather than making you pick products one by one, since that is where the double work creeps back in. FYI I built LabelCraft, a barcode label app that works from both of those inputs. Custom-Cursor July 19, 2026, 4:52pm 9 Hey @Wildernest1 , hope you are doing well! I agree native barcode label printing from Purchase Orders would make the receiving workflow much more efficient and improve inventory accuracy. YoBeCo August 13, 2026, 11:09pm 10 Adding to this, based on testing it hands-on this week. Native POs aren’t readable directly, that part is right, there’s no PurchaseOrder object in the Admin API. But merchants on the native PO flow aren’t stuck, because the PO flow has no independent receiving. When you create a PO in the admin and link a transfer, Shopify auto-creates the shipment once it goes in transit, and you receive against that. So the receive event lands on an InventoryShipment either way. I tested this end to end: created a PO, linked the transfer, received 6 of 10 through the admin flow. The API showed acceptedQuantity=6 on the line, and origin.name came back as the supplier name from the PO. So an app can show “delivery from [supplier]” and print exact received quantities with no CSV step, even for merchants who only ever think in POs. Worth knowing if you’re evaluating tools: the question isn’t really whether it supports POs, it’s whether it reads the shipment the PO produced. Disclosure: I’m building in this space too (LabelDock, in review right now). Philip_Rose August 15, 2026, 1:35am 11 Late addition, with the same disclosure as the others in this thread — I build in this space too ( LabelLoom , on the App Store). The InventoryShipment finding above is genuinely useful — if your POs live in Shopify and you receive through the linked transfer, that path has you covered, and it’s good news the received quantities turn out to be readable after all. The case I built for is the one that never touches Shopify at all: the delivery that arrives with a supplier spreadsheet or a paper packing note — no PO or transfer in the admin anywhere. You paste or CSV-import the list (SKUs + quantities, partial deliveries fine), it matches your catalogue, loudly flags anything it can’t find instead of silently dropping it, and prints to Dymo/Zebra/Avery presets scan-tested on the physical printers. It’ll also generate barcodes for products that don’t have one yet, without ever overwriting existing ones. Until Stocky switches off on 31 August every label is free — the meter only starts in September — so it costs nothing to test whichever tool matches where your deliveries actually live. Lillianruan August 21, 2026, 4:51am 12 Definitely. Barcode labels at receiving make a huge difference once you’re handling more inventory. If you don’t want to wait for Shopify to add it natively, have a look at Lofko. It’s built more around the inventory/warehouse side of the workflow, so receiving, barcodes and stock management can all sit in the same process. kingstore August 23, 2026, 1:48am 13 Yes this would certainly help many stores who need labels as they go. Likely this will come with time. Shopifys own label printer does let you print off a list of barcodes for SKUs so what you could do is export the PO, then use this as a starting place to ‘import the SKUs’ into the Retail Barcode Labels - Create and print barcode labels for your products | Shopify App Store What you’d want to do in this case, for large POs at least is tag the items in the PO, then use that tag to determine which products need to be printed. Alternatively, you can use an app like SKUSavvy AI Powered WMS - AI powered mobile WMS to streamline inventory and ship faster | Shopify App Store which has native printing directly from the PO put-away enabling you to select all, counted quantities, received quantities, or individual. skusavvy-print-po-items 2804×1860 285 KB Hope that helps! jmiralles August 24, 2026, 7:34am 14 he reason none of the apps here can print from your Shopify PO is that purchase orders aren’t exposed in the Admin API. An app can read products, variants and inventory, but not the PO you created in the admin. So every tool in this thread works the same way: the PO lives in the app, and the labels come from there. Two things worth checking before you pick one, because that’s where the duplicate work actually comes from: 1. Does it print from received quantities or ordered ones? If 40 of 100 arrive, you want 40 labels, not 100 — otherwise you’re re-counting by hand anyway, which is the thing you were trying to avoid. 2. Does it fall back to the SKU when a variant has no barcode? Most catalogues have a few, and a silently skipped label is worse than a wrong one: you find out at the shelf. Disclosure: I build EasyRestock, which works that way — one label per unit received, or per unit ordered if nothing has been received yet, on A4 sheets or 57×32 rolls. Same trade-off as everyone else here: the PO lives in the app, not in Shopify’s own PO screen. YoBeCo August 25, 2026, 2:46pm 15 Following up on my post above, since Stocky goes off this week. On the point just above about every tool working the same way, with the PO living in the app: the first half is right, there’s no PurchaseOrder object in the Admin API, so nothing can read the PO document itself. But that isn’t the only way out, and there’s a third path that needs no re-entry and no CSV. When you create a PO in the Shopify admin and link a transfer, Shopify auto-creates a shipment once that transfer goes in transit, and receiving happens against that shipment. The shipment is exposed through the API, and its line items carry the accepted, rejected and unreceived quantities, with the supplier name on the transfer origin. I tested it end to end: received 6 of 10 through the normal admin flow, and the API returned acceptedQuantity=6 with origin.name set to the supplier from the PO. So you can keep creating purchase orders exactly where you do today, in Shopify, and still print labels for what actually arrived. The app reads the shipment your PO produced, rather than a second copy of the PO kept somewhere else. Disclosure, same as everyone else here: I build LabelDock, which went live on the App Store today. MyWorks August 25, 2026, 6:22pm 16 Feel free to give Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Purchase orders, inventory management, reporting, COGS + more | Shopify App Store a try? We’ve built it completely free for Shopify merchants; and it includes quite a bit of functionality around barcodes and labels - both in terms of supporting barcode scanners, as well as label printing! You can customize how you want the label to look, and easily print from products, POs, and more. juhyun_han September 14, 2026, 1:04am 17 @Wildernest1 @MDS73 — @Clement_Foltzer ’s point is the structural one: Transfers are in the Admin API and native purchase orders are not, so the PO screen cannot get a print button from a third party no matter who builds it. Worth adding what that means for anything you do buy, and one trap in the workflow itself that decides whether the labels are any use. Print from what arrived, not from what was ordered. Almost every version of this prints the PO line quantity, because that is the number on the screen when you raise the order. Partial deliveries then break it. Twelve ordered, five turn up, you print twelve labels — seven loose labels now exist for stock that is not in the building. They get used on the next delivery, which is the right product at the wrong cost, or they go in a drawer and somebody sticks them on in six weeks. The label has to come off the receipt event, per line, at the quantity actually counted in. Two consequences of that worth checking before you pay for anything: Does it label the partial, and can it label the remainder later? A receiving workflow that only prints once per PO is unusable for anyone whose supplier short-ships, which is everyone. Which cost does the label’s row carry? If the app prints from the ordered cost and the invoice arrives above the order — a supplier raising a price between quote and delivery is routine and nobody is told — the barcode scans fine while your cost record is wrong. That error is invisible until you look at margin a month later and cannot explain it. And the caution about the API gap, since it is the thing that will surprise you: because native POs are not exposed, any app that does this keeps its own purchase orders rather than reading yours. That is not a flaw, it is the only option available — but it means your PO history then lives in two places, and the app’s view of what has been received can drift from Shopify’s inventory if anyone adjusts stock outside it. Before buying, the question I would ask is what happens when the two disagree, and whether the app can tell you that they do. Disclosure: I build an inventory app with its own purchase orders, so I have an interest and the above describes a limitation of my own design as much as anyone’s. @FlochForster ’s app already covers the transfers-and-CSV route with a free tier, which is the path that actually works today. It was a quick and easy way to create barcoded labels for all received stock items Technical Q&A customizations AI-generated summary Merchants are looking for a replacement workflow for Stocky’s CSV export used to print barcode labels for newly received inventory in Shopify POS locations. The main gap identified is that Shopify’s native Purchase Orders do not currently provide a clean CSV of only the items actually received, which matters especially for partial deliveries. Key points raised: A full PO export can overprint labels because it reflects ordered quantities, not received quantities. The preferred data source should be the receipt, transfer, or shipment lines showing what arrived. Essential CSV fields suggested include barcode, product title, variant, retail price, and quantity received; barcodes should be treated as text to preserve leading zeros. Several workaround paths were proposed, including exporting inventory data, using supplier packing-list CSVs, or adopting third-party apps that support PO receiving, Stocky migration, barcode check-in, direct label printing, or CSV/PDF/Dymo/Zebra output. No native Shopify solution or confirmed CSV feature was announced. The issue remains open, with the practical resolution being third-party tools or manual export workflows for now. PBN1 June 10, 2026, 5:45pm 1 Since Stocky is going away will there be a way to get a csv download of received items in the new PO creation link under Products. Stocky is currently the only quick way to create barcode labels for incoming stock for POS locations. Pipokx June 10, 2026, 7:04pm 2 Hey @PBN1 , Indeed, there is a major operational gap right now when it comes to barcode printing workflow. To figure out the cleanest way to extract and route that data for you, I’d look into two things: Your Printing Setup: Once you have the CSV of received items, what software or hardware are you using to actually generate the labels (e.g., Dymo, Zebra, Shopify’s Retail Barcode app)? Partial Deliveries: If a PO is only partially delivered, do you need the CSV to strictly isolate the newly received units, or the entire original PO? Curious to hear how you are handling the transition! Thanks, Julien Clement_Foltzer June 25, 2026, 7:20am 4 Disclosure up front: I build LabelCraft. The CSV export-then-reimport dance is exactly the gap Stocky left. LabelCraft reads a received Transfer or Shipment directly and prints exact-size labels for every line item, so there’s no CSV step at all. It also prints from a pasted or uploaded SKU list if you’d rather skip Transfers, and generates a valid GS1/EAN-13 for anything missing a barcode so it scans at the till. Free up to 200 labels a month if you want to try it on your next received batch. Whatever you land on, export your Stocky data before Aug 31, it doesn’t migrate automatically. MyWorks July 9, 2026, 9:49pm 5 If it helps, we do support label printing in the PO app we recently built - completely free, to help merchants as Stocky goes away. We think Shopify merchants deserve a robust, stable and long term way to handle Purchase Orders in a way that fits their business. DougInOr July 12, 2026, 5:00pm 7 I don’t think a CSV output will happen under the native POs. You can though either utilize Stocky’s API, download those POs into a CSV now using Stocky’s download feature (pain the the …) or just move to an app that has a migration from Stocky using their API. Using an app that does have a Stocky API integration (like FyreTrail ’s Stocky Migration Tool), you can download your delivered POs, your incoming POs, Suppliers and Adjustments into FyreTrail and then print labels directly from the PO for items that you receive. There’s a ton of flexibility to get your data out of Stocky and into FyreTrail in plenty of time and you can simply pick up where you left off (many stores who use FyreTrail have done just that). If you choose to do that you will get a solid replacement in FyreTrail that has more intelligence built in to the day to day operations that you previously did in Stocky. If you just want to print labels then the 2 other apps (LabelCraft and FlochForster) are likely great solutions for you as well. Clement_Foltzer July 12, 2026, 7:25pm 8 Quick follow-up since this thread picked back up (still the LabelCraft founder). @FlochForster puts a finger on the real pain: partial deliveries. Exporting the whole PO gives you labels for the ordered quantities, not for what actually arrived. That is exactly why we read the received lines of a native Transfer or Shipment instead of the PO: one label per unit actually received in this delivery, nothing else. @PBN1 if you already have a Stocky CSV and want to sanity-check what will print before touching anything: we put a free, no-install checker at labelcraft.tech/stocky-label-preview. Paste the CSV, it previews the labels and flags missing or non-scannable barcodes. No account needed. On the Stocky API route @DougInOr mentions: agreed, that is the clean path for PO history. For the label half specifically you do not need history, just the received lines going forward. haloxzk July 20, 2026, 3:57am 9 Hi @PBN1 - I am researching the receiving-to-label workflow after Stocky, not promoting an app. I tested Shopify Transfers and found that basic received-quantity label printing is already covered, so I am trying to understand the remaining CSV gap. For your most recent delivery, did the CSV need to come from Shopify’s native PO, or would a supplier packing-list CSV have worked? Which exception took the most time: a partial receipt, a SKU mismatch, or a missing barcode? If you are comfortable sharing only an anonymized header row or 5-20 rows with fake values, I can turn it into a no-cost reconciliation mockup and send the result back for feedback. kingstore August 23, 2026, 4:15am 10 @PBN1 Native Purchase Orders still do not give you a clean CSV of what you just received so you can print barcode labels the way Stocky did. That gap is real. Workarounds people use: Export inventory (or the products you care about) and feed your label software from that, not from the PO receive screen. On partial deliveries, filter to what actually arrived or use a tool that treats each receipt as its own label batch. A full PO export labels ordered qty, not received qty. Some label apps pull barcodes from Shopify products without Stocky. If your flow is receive on the floor then print labels for what hit the shelf, a warehouse app that does scan receive plus labels in one pass is usually less painful than CSV glue. I work on SKUSavvy which handles barcode check-in and labels as part of the floor workflow (plus bin put-away if you need it). Free plan available, paid plans start at $19/month with a 14 day free trial. replenly.app Replenly — purchase orders and reorder forecasting for Shopify Know what to reorder today. Purchase orders, receiving, barcode stocktakes and Stocky CSV import, from $0. Denyslg September 5, 2026, 4:27am 12 Now that the thread has settled the CSV should come from what arrived rather than what you ordered, the columns decide whether it prints. Five of them. Barcode, exactly as it sits on the variant and formatted as text, or Excel eats the leading zeros. Product title, and the variant in its own column, because “Blue / M” glued onto a long title wraps and ruins the alignment on a small label. Retail price, since a label without one sends staff back to a screen. Quantity received, which is how many labels to print, not how many you ordered. Then the format question. A Dymo or Zebra path sends each label at true size as you receive, one line at a time. A PDF sheet suits labelling a whole delivery at a bench, and fails the day a driver scales it to 96 percent and scanners start rejecting the quiet zones. Philip_Rose July 8, 2026, 12:58am 20 Coming at this from the developer side, so take it with that context: the reason nothing has fully replaced the “print from a confirmed PO” flow is structural, there’s still no Purchase Order API, so apps simply can’t see PO data at all. Neither needs the missing API, which is the point. And on where native POs fall short most, from what I’ve seen with migrating retailers, it’s the receiving end. Ordered is received — partial deliveries are the norm — and the moment stock lands you need labels printed for what’s actually in the box. That whole step just isn’t in the native flow. If Shopify does ship a PO API later, these workarounds can presumably plug into it. But with the August cut off, I wouldn’t plan a migration around waiting for it. This is surely good news for everyone building around this gap, since every work around discussed above can plug into it, once it ships. One timing caveat worth stating plainly: a conference session in a couple of weeks means schemas and previews, not a GA API — anyone migrating off Stocky before 31 August still shouldn’t plan around waiting for it. By the way, congratulations to MyWorks on shipping Stockroom — a free PO + receiving flow with label printing built in is a strong answer for stores that want the whole lifecycle in one place. After this thread’s developments, the remaining gap cases are narrower but real: deliveries whose paperwork never enters a PO system at all (supplier spreadsheets, emailed packing notes), and stores that need more control over the labels themselves — custom sizes, layouts, roll printers. That’s where the label-first tools still earn their keep. Between an API on the horizon, free PO apps, and the label apps, the post-Stocky picture finally looks less scary than it did in February. text: Stocky Alternatives = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="chat_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-ai_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-events_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-gamification_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="discourse-reactions_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="poll_desktop" /> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="9" data-theme-name="header submenus"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="14" data-theme-name="right sidebar blocks"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="7" data-theme-name="shopify"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="40" data-theme-name="custom: set image dimensions"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="19" data-theme-name="header submenus (custom styling rules)"/> = 40rem)" rel="stylesheet" data-target="desktop_theme" data-theme-id="31" data-theme-name="hotfix: misc"/> Shopify Community Stocky Alternatives Shopify Discussion customizations , troubleshooting MurphysBootShop June 10, 2026, 8:00pm 1 The sundowning of Stocky in August feels like a nightmare right now. My business doesn’t distinguish between vendors and suppliers when purchasing so going to Shopify’s native purchase order interface also means creating supplier profiles for all the vendors even though all of my products are already associated with the correct vendors. Has anyone made an app that does EXACTLY what stocky does? I’m desperate for a budget option that can generate POs from specific vendors and utilize filters during generation. Thanks! DougInOr June 10, 2026, 10:27pm 2 Exactly, no. That would flirt with trademark/copyright infringement. However, FyreTrail is likely something you need to look into simply because it handles the Purchase Order flow really well. The key difference between Stocky and FyreTrail is that Stocky (as I see it) handled Shopify’s product catalog for retailers whereas FyreTrail handles retailers and removes the concern about Shopify’s catalog from retailers. FyreTrail approaches the process for retailers who need to order products from their Suppliers. It recognizes a “Vendor” really is a Supplier (who sells the item to you) and a Brand (what sells to a Supplier or you) and doesn’t do the silly things that Stocky does with making you choose a Supplier or a Vendor when creating a PO. On top of that, it also recognizes that your Products shouldn’t have to be recreated 15 times to get them into Shopify. Do it once - on the PO and doesn’t force you to enter the things you don’t need to know to get a product ordered. Worry about that when it gets here and when you’re ready to sell it, not when you want to order it. So, FyreTrail is process oriented… to YOUR process… with a little help along the way. Give it a look then reach out if you have any questions. oscprofessional June 11, 2026, 12:34pm 3 Hi @MurphysBootShop , Apps Similar to Stocky Lokad (formerly known for demand forecasting) PO generation from vendors Inventory-based filters Budget: ~$200-500/month (not cheap) Infoplus (Inventory + PO Management) Vendor-based PO generation Advanced filtering Budget: ~$300+/month TraceLink for Shopify (Enterprise) Supply chain PO management Vendor management Budget: Custom pricing (pricey) SealSubs-Roan June 14, 2026, 5:12am 5 MurphysBootShop: The sundowning of Stocky in August feels like a nightmare right now. My business doesn’t distinguish between vendors and suppliers when purchasing so going to Shopify’s native purchase order interface also means creating supplier profiles for all the vendors even though all of my products are already associated with the correct vendors. Has anyone made an app that does EXACTLY what stocky does? I’m desperate for a budget option that can generate POs from specific vendors and utilize filters during generation. Hey there @MurphysBootShop Several merchants share that the best way around this is to abandon Stocky’s vendor system and use vendor tags or metafields to organize the product information, and then place the orders through a third party system that uses filtering logic. Solutions like Cin7 Core, Sumtracker, or Katana are usually the best alternatives to Stocky’s PO creation and vendor-specific filtering. They provide you the ability to group products dynamically and generate POs without having to recreate supplier records as you must on the Shopify native app. And if you really want to keep it light, using tagged products with bulk export apps like Matrixify (formerly Excelify) can also simulate the basics of a PO workflow. Pipokx June 14, 2026, 8:55am 6 Hey @MurphysBootShop , What type of business do you run and what volumes you process ? Depending on your business specificities, some apps will be better than others, or sometimes, no apps at all are needed as jobs can be done in the background using logic and syncs between your systems. Tell us a bit more about your business and workflow, Thanks MurphysBootShop June 18, 2026, 5:32pm 7 I run a small shoe store which means that frequently I am ordering 2-12 pairs at a time. Currently when using Stocky: I will select a vendor, under “forecast type” I use “target stock level” and set it to 1, apply a filter to only add items with a relevant tag, and then create the PO. Being able to limit my PO’s reach by tags is crucial as my store’s inventory contains dozens of styles and odd sizes I normally have no intention of ordering. kingstore June 19, 2026, 8:43pm 8 I’m certainly biased but the best solution for the Stocky sunset is SKUSavvy. Stocky has a lot of logic based components and SKUSavvy is designed to mimic nearly exactly what stocky does. This includes automated purchase orders with min/max levels, automated allocation of stock across your locations, check-in barcode scanning and printing, complete inventory management with 3D bin mapping and bin-to-bin replenishment, as well as guided pick routing, fulfillment and shipping automation. Additionally, SKUSavvy is perfectly integrated with Shopify providing a dual way sync across all key data types and for all Shopify versions and POS. While this is not a perfect replacement, if you are looking for the de facto replacement for Stocky, this will certainly do it. This is not free, so its hard to complete there, but at $179/month for a full WMS, this is also not break the bank type of system. Give it a try for free or explore the website MurphysBootShop July 8, 2026, 3:00pm 9 Yeah, I’m not even gonna remotely consider a solution that costs more than $100 per month. We pay so much for shopify already, I can’t justify more than $1000 to our yearly operating costs for a piece of functionality that used to be free on this POS and our previous system. kthoppae July 9, 2026, 3:38pm 12 that makes sense. It sounds like the biggest hurdle isn’t learning a new purchasing workflow it’s having to recreate operational relationships that already existed. If your replenishment process already knows which products belong to which vendor, having to manually assign suppliers across the catalog before you can even generate a PO creates a lot of upfront work before you see any benefit. It seems like preserving those supplier relationships during the transition is almost as important as the PO functionality itself. MurphysBootShop July 9, 2026, 3:53pm 13 I agree. But I transitioned to Shopify 3 years ago and I can’t really start over. What do you recommend? kthoppae July 9, 2026, 4:19pm 14 That’s a tough spot, and I probably wouldn’t start over by manually rebuilding everything either. If I were evaluating replacements today, I’d focus less on feature checklists and more on migration effort. A few questions I’d ask are: • Can it preserve or import existing supplier relationships? • Can it generate POs using the workflow I’m already familiar with? • Does it support receiving and inventory updates without adding extra manual work? • How much catalog setup is required before I can create my first PO? If a solution requires weeks of rebuilding master data before it delivers value, that migration cost becomes part of the decision too. Out of curiosity, roughly how many SKUs are you managing today? DougInOr July 9, 2026, 9:23pm 15 I’m going to tack on to @kthoppae 's evaluation, but I really think any valid solution needs to give you an easy way to transition from Stocky. The caveat to you not wanting to spend money on an app for features that used to be free with Pro is that many inexpensive solutions don’t offer an easy transition system. And, if they do, the functionality you need is lacking. I’m not calling any single app out at all (I’m not even thinking of any), but the reality just boils down to how much money an app needs to make simply to be viable. Ok, so it’s a tradeoff… you want an easy transition? Might be hard to find an app that gives you this and gives you the features you NEED for the cost that you’re willing to digest. I’m not trying to get you to come to FyreTrail… I’m really not. I would love to have you, but if FyreTrail is not something you’re even wanting to look at because it costs money then I get it - your priority is then budget and that’s completely fair and understandable. But… what it does do is save you time both in the migration (we have one) and the day to day uses that it will very likely pay for itself many times over. Ultimately it’s totally your choice to either take that risk after the 14 day free trial or recognize it during the trial and take advantage of it afterwards. So what if it’s not FyreTrail? Evaluate, weigh your options, weigh the amount of work you do now and in the future, then decide, “Is this worth my money given what it does for me?” Then choose the app or direction that meets those needs best. You’re first, your store is first, not some app (yes, even my app) that can’t meet those needs. MyWorks July 10, 2026, 8:16pm 16 @MurphysBootShop just wanted to add a comment here that’s hopefully helpful - and isn’t a paid solution. With Stocky going away, and our own users asking us for a robust way to handle POs and light inventory management / reordering with Shopify; we decided to build our own solution, but for free. Check it out at Stockroom - Stockroom ‑ Purchase Orders - Unlimited purchase orders, receiving & sync with QuickBooks | Shopify App Store - we’re making it completely free for everyone! We think Shopify merchants deserve a robust, stable and long term way to handle Purchase Orders (and the re-ordering/receiving processes that come with them) in a way that fits their business, and not at an additional cost. We’d love to hear any feedback as we continue to build more features to make this a helpful home for Shopify store merchants coming from Stocky!
